1.1.guide_fact: Chance is random variation that produces conclusions differing from the true results, and a study with few patients is especially likely to give a misleading impression of the wider population.

expls.Selection bias: Selection bias is a systematic problem in how the compared groups were assembled, so they differ in more than the treatment. A small number of patients does not make the groups systematically different; it makes the result vulnerable to random variation, which is chance.
expls.Measurement bias: Measurement bias is a systematic error from the way an outcome or exposure is measured, such as unstandardized methods or unequal detection between groups. The number of patients says nothing about how pain was measured; too few patients is a problem of random variation instead.
expls.Confounding: Confounding needs a covariate that is associated with both the treatment and the outcome so its effect cannot be separated from the treatment effect. A statement about having few patients names no such covariate; the concern is random variation, which is chance.
expls.Chance: Correct. Chance is random variation producing conclusions that differ from the true results, and a small sample can give a misleading impression of the population it came from. Statistical analysis can estimate chance, and good design reduces it, but it is never totally eliminated.
expls.External validity (generalizability): External validity is the degree to which results also hold true in other patients and clinical settings. The worry here is different: with so few patients, random variation may make even the observed difference misleading, and that is chance rather than generalizability.

1.2.guide_fact: External validity (generalizability) is the degree to which results are also true in other clinical settings and patients, so results from a study of men may not apply to a woman.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 50
1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 51

expls.Selection bias: Selection bias concerns how the compared groups inside a study were assembled so that they differ in more than the treatment. Both treatment groups were all men, so sex does not make them differ; the limitation is who the findings apply to.
expls.Measurement bias: Measurement bias is incorrect results caused by the method of measurement. Nothing about how pain was measured is described; the point is that a study done only in men may not apply to a woman, which is a question of generalizability.
expls.Confounding: Confounding needs a covariate that differs between the treatment groups and is tied to both treatment and outcome. Every patient was a man in both groups, so sex cannot differ between them and cannot confound; it only limits applying the results to a woman.
expls.Chance: Chance is random variation that produces results differing from the truth. The concern here is not random error in the men studied but whether these patients, all men, represent this patient, a woman.
expls.External validity (generalizability): Correct. External validity, also called generalizability, is the degree to which results are also true in other clinical settings and patients. Applying a study of men to a woman assumes surgery works the same way in both sexes, and this is rarely settled by a single study.

1.3.guide_fact: Measurement bias occurs when participants in one group are more likely than those in another to have their outcome detected, as when more surgically treated than medically treated patients remain under care to have pain measured.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 41

expls.Selection bias: Selection bias concerns how the compared groups were assembled, and here the groups were formed by referral for surgery or not. Fewer medically treated patients remaining under care is a different problem: the pain outcome could not be observed equally in the two groups, which makes measurement bias the better fit.
expls.Measurement bias: Correct. Measurement bias means participants in one group are more likely than another to have their outcome detected. All the surgically treated patients but only 10 of 18 medically treated patients stayed under care, so pain was not measured with equal completeness in the two groups.
expls.Confounding: Confounding needs a covariate that is associated with both treatment and outcome. Unequal follow-up is not a patient characteristic that travels with treatment and recovery; it is a difference in how completely the outcome could be observed, which is a measurement problem.
expls.Chance: Chance is random variation, equally likely to push a result higher or lower. Fewer medically treated patients remaining under care is a systematic difference between the groups in outcome detection, so it is bias, not chance.
expls.External validity (generalizability): External validity asks whether results apply to other patients and settings. Unequal follow-up affects whether the results are correct for the patients who were actually studied, which makes it a threat to internal validity, not generalizability.

1.4.guide_fact: Selection bias occurs when comparisons are made between groups that differ in more than the focus of the study, for example when patients healthy enough to tolerate surgery form the surgical group.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 40

expls.Selection bias: Correct. Selection bias occurs when compared groups differ in more than the focus of the study. Patients referred for surgery were younger and fitter, so better recovery may reflect who was chosen for surgery rather than what surgery did.
expls.Measurement bias: Measurement bias comes from the way an outcome is measured. Age and fitness describe how the patients who were referred differ from those who were not, which is about how the groups were assembled and not about how pain was measured.
expls.Confounding: Age and fitness could act as covariates, but confounding is the inability to separate a covariate's effect from the studied variable during analysis, and it can itself result from selection bias. The statement stresses which patients were referred to surgery, which is how the groups were selected, so selection bias is the better description.
expls.Chance: Chance is random variation, which would not consistently place younger, fitter patients in the surgical group. A consistent difference in the kind of patients in the two groups is systematic, so it is bias rather than chance.
expls.External validity (generalizability): External validity concerns applying results to other populations. A difference between the two treatment groups inside the study threatens internal validity, the degree to which results are correct for the patients studied, not generalizability.

1.5.guide_fact: Measurement bias occurs when the method of measurement leads to incorrect results, such as when outcomes are reported or recorded differently in the compared groups.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 41

expls.Selection bias: Selection bias concerns how patients ended up in each group. This statement is about how pain was reported and recorded after treatment, which is the measurement of the outcome and not the assembly of the groups.
expls.Measurement bias: Correct. Measurement bias means the method of measuring leads to incorrect results, including when one group is less likely to have its outcome detected. If surgical patients reported less pain and physicians recorded less pain for them, the outcome was measured unequally between the groups.
expls.Confounding: Confounding involves a covariate associated with both treatment and outcome. Differences in how pain is reported and recorded are errors in obtaining the outcome measurement itself, not a patient characteristic linked to both treatment and recovery.
expls.Chance: Chance is random variation, equally likely to push results higher or lower. Systematically less reporting and less recording of pain in one group pushes results in a single direction, which is bias rather than chance.
expls.External validity (generalizability): External validity is about whether results hold in other patients and settings. Unequal reporting and recording of pain undermines whether the results are correct for the patients studied, which is internal validity.

1.6.guide_fact: Confounding occurs when the effect of a covariate cannot be separated from the effect of the variable being studied because the covariate is associated with both the exposure and the outcome.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 42

expls.Selection bias: Selection bias is bias in how the groups were assembled. The statement names a third variable, absence of other medical conditions, that is tied to both receiving surgery and recovering; that pattern defines confounding, even though confounding can sometimes result from selection bias.
expls.Measurement bias: Measurement bias comes from incorrect or unequal measurement of the outcome or exposure. Nothing here concerns how recovery was measured; the problem is that another medical condition is related to both treatment and outcome.
expls.Confounding: Correct. Confounding occurs when a covariate is associated with both the exposure and the outcome, so its effect cannot be separated from the effect of the treatment. Having no other medical conditions makes patients more likely to be referred for surgery and more likely to recover, and it could explain the difference by itself.
expls.Chance: Chance is random variation with no consistent direction. Absence of other conditions is a specific factor that pushes both surgical referral and recovery in the same direction, so this is a systematic covariate effect, not chance.
expls.External validity (generalizability): External validity asks whether results extend to other patients and settings. A covariate that distorts the treatment comparison inside the study threatens internal validity, whether the results are correct for the patients studied.

1.7.guide_fact: That histamine mediates inflammation in allergic rhinitis supports a promising hypothesis that antihistamines will relieve symptoms, but the hypothesis must be tested by studying effects on symptoms in patients with allergic rhinitis.

expls.Drugs that block the effects of histamin: This states as fact what is only a hypothesis. Knowing histamine mediates inflammation makes blocking it a promising idea, but whether blocking it actually relieves symptoms must be tested in people who have hay fever.
expls.A fall in histamine levels in the nose i: A fall in nasal histamine is an intermediate biologic outcome, and such measures are not shown to be reliable markers of clinical success. What matters to patients is relief of symptoms such as itchy nose, sneezing and congestion, which must be measured directly.
expls.Antihistamines may be effective, and the: Correct. The fact that histamine mediates inflammation leads to a promising hypothesis that antihistamines may work, but it must be tested. Their effects on symptoms such as itchy nose, sneezing and congestion should be studied in patients with allergic rhinitis.
This assumes more than the fact given. Histamine is only one of many mediators of inflammation in hay fever, so other mediators may well matter to the symptoms.
expls.If laboratory studies of disease are con: Convincing laboratory findings can suggest a hypothesis, but they do not show that patients benefit. The hypothesis still needs to be tested in people with the disease, so clinical research remains necessary.

1.7.correct: Antihistamines may be effective, and their effects on symptoms (e.g., itchy nose, sneezing, and congestion) should be studied in patients with allergic rhinitis.

expls.Samples of populations may have characte: This statement is true, so it is not the incorrect one. Even when correct sampling procedures are followed, a sample can differ from its population by chance, which is random variation producing results that differ from the truth.
expls.Samples of populations are the only feas: This statement is true, so it is not the incorrect one. A population is all the people in a defined setting, which is generally impractical to study in full, so a subset of it, a sample, is what gets studied.
expls.When populations are correctly sampled,: Correct: this is the incorrect statement. expls.Given these studies, the decision about: Correct. Applying results from younger patients to a 72-year-old is generalizing beyond the people studied, which is external validity. It is a matter of personal judgment informed by whatever is known about whether older patients respond as younger ones do; generalizability is rarely settled by a single study.
expls.Relying on these studies for your patien: Relying on studies of other kinds of patients is a question of external validity, also called generalizability. Internal validity is the degree to which results are correct for the sample of patients who were actually studied.
expls.The results in these studies are affecte: Chance and bias can both affect how correct the results are for the patients studied. Chance is random variation and bias is systematic error, and the two can coexist, so a study cannot be assumed free of bias.

1.10.guide_fact: A difference in coronary events cannot be explained by exercise if the two groups exercised the same amount, whereas differences between the groups before the study (selection bias) or in how the outcome was detected (measurement bias) can produce such a finding.

expls.The volunteers did not actually increase: Correct: this is the least likely explanation. If volunteers exercised no more than nonvolunteers, exercise could not account for a difference in coronary heart disease. The other explanations involve group differences or unequal detection of the outcome, which can produce the finding.
expls.The volunteers were at higher risk for d: This is a likely explanation, so it is not the least likely one. If volunteers were at higher risk before the study began, the groups differed in more than the exercise program, which is selection bias, and it could produce higher rates in the exercise group.
expls.Volunteers got more checkups, and silent: This is a likely explanation, so it is not the least likely one. Volunteers had more checkups, so silent myocardial infarctions were more likely to be found in them; the outcome was detected unequally between groups, which is measurement bias.

1.10.correct: The volunteers did not actually increase their exercise and the amount of exercise was the same in the two groups.

1.11.guide_fact: Outcomes should include both biologic and clinical outcomes; for a new drug the effect on the clinical outcome, such as the rate of sudden death, matters most, because an intermediate biologic outcome such as fewer arrhythmias can be an unreliable marker of it.

A mechanism of action explains how a drug might work, but it does not show that patients benefit. What matters for prescribing is whether the drug changes the clinical outcome, here sudden death.
expls.How well the drug prevents ventricular p: Suppressing ventricular premature depolarizations is an intermediate biologic outcome, and it can be an unreliable marker of the clinical outcome. Some arrhythmia-suppressing drugs have actually increased the rate of sudden death, so this result alone does not show benefit.
expls.The rate of sudden death in similar peop: Correct. The drug's effect on mortality is the most important thing to determine, so the rate of sudden death in similar people who do and do not take it is what you want. A drug can improve an intermediate biologic outcome yet still increase sudden death.

1.11.correct: The rate of sudden death in similar people who do and do not take the drug.

1.12.guide_fact: Recall bias, a measurement bias, occurs when people with an illness remember or report earlier exposures differently because they suspect those exposures caused their illness.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 41

expls.Selection bias: Selection bias concerns how the compared groups were assembled. The concern here is that women with thrombophlebitis remembered and reported contraceptive use more completely, which is a problem in how exposure information was obtained.
expls.Measurement bias: Correct. Asking people about a past exposure relies on memory, and recall bias occurs when those with the illness recall exposures they think are related to it more completely. That makes the exposure measured unequally in the two groups, so it is measurement bias.
expls.Confounding: Confounding needs a covariate associated with both the exposure and the outcome. Fuller recall by women who are ill is not a separate factor tied to both; it is an error in obtaining the exposure information.
expls.Chance: Chance is random variation with no consistent direction. Women with the illness reporting contraceptive use more completely pushes the results in one direction, which is a systematic error rather than chance.
expls.External validity (generalizability): External validity asks whether the findings apply to other patients and settings. More complete reporting by ill women distorts the results for the women studied, which is a threat to internal validity.

1.13.guide_fact: Measurement bias occurs when one group is more likely to have its exposure or outcome detected or recorded than another, for example when clinicians question and record contraceptive use more carefully in women who have the disease.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 41

expls.Selection bias: Selection bias concerns how the groups were assembled. Here the groups already exist; the problem is that clinicians asked about and recorded contraceptive use more carefully in women with thrombophlebitis, which is unequal measurement of exposure.
expls.Measurement bias: Correct. Measurement bias occurs when information is not obtained the same way in both groups. Clinicians who knew estrogen can cause clotting questioned and recorded contraceptive use more carefully in women with thrombophlebitis, so exposure was measured unequally.
expls.Confounding: Confounding requires a covariate linked to both exposure and outcome. More careful questioning by doctors is not such a covariate; it is a difference in how the exposure information was collected and recorded.
expls.Chance: Chance is random variation with no consistent direction. Doctors questioning and recording more carefully in only one group systematically inflates the reported exposure in that group, which is bias rather than chance.
expls.External validity (generalizability): External validity is about whether results extend to other patients and settings. Unequal questioning affects whether the results are correct for the women studied, which is internal validity.

1.14.guide_fact: Chance is random variation producing conclusions that differ from the true results, and small numbers of participants increase the possibility that chance accounts for differences between groups.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 47

expls.Selection bias: Selection bias is a systematic difference in how groups were assembled. A small number of women does not by itself make the groups differ systematically; it makes the observed difference more likely to arise by random variation, which is chance.
expls.Measurement bias: Measurement bias is a systematic error in how exposure or outcome is measured. The number of women in the study has no bearing on how contraceptive use was measured; small numbers threaten the result through random variation.
expls.Confounding: Confounding requires a covariate tied to both exposure and outcome. Small size does not identify any such covariate; it raises the possibility that a difference between groups arose by random variation.
expls.Chance: Correct. Chance is random variation producing conclusions that differ from the true results, and small numbers of participants increase the possibility that chance accounts for a difference between groups. Statistical analysis can estimate the role of chance.
expls.External validity (generalizability): External validity concerns whether results apply to other patients and settings. Having few participants raises doubt about whether the observed difference is real even for the women studied, which is a problem of chance.

1.15.guide_fact: Selection bias occurs when the compared groups differ in more than the focus of the study, such as when cases and comparison patients come from different neighborhoods that differ in socioeconomic and other factors.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 40

expls.Selection bias: Correct. Selection bias occurs when compared groups differ in more than the focus of the study. Women admitted by doctors in different neighborhoods likely differ in socioeconomic and other characteristics related to health outcomes, so the groups were not comparable to begin with.
expls.Measurement bias: Measurement bias comes from how exposure or outcome is measured. Nothing here says contraceptive use was recorded differently; the statement describes who came to be in each group through admission by doctors in different neighborhoods.
expls.Confounding: Confounding is a covariate whose effect cannot be separated from the exposure's effect at analysis. The statement does not name a covariate tied to both contraceptive use and thrombophlebitis; it describes how the two groups came to be assembled, which is selection.
expls.Chance: Chance is random variation without a consistent direction. Groups drawn from different neighborhoods differ systematically in characteristics related to health, so this is a bias in the groups, not random variation.
expls.External validity (generalizability): External validity asks whether results extend to other patients and settings. Groups that differ before the comparison begins threaten whether the results are correct for the women studied, which is internal validity.

2.1.guide_fact: Incidence density measures new cases over time in a changing (dynamic) population, with a denominator of person-time, such as new cases per 100,000 people per year from a cancer registry.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17
3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

expls.Point prevalence: That is wrong: point prevalence counts existing cases at one moment, while a cancer registry counts new cases arising over a year, so the numerator here is new diagnoses, not cases already present.
expls.Incidence density: Correct. Registries count new cases over a year in a dynamic population, where men are constantly entering and leaving the census population, so the denominator is person-time and the rate is an incidence density.
expls.Period prevalence: That is wrong: period prevalence counts all cases present during a span of time, including old ones, but a registry rate of new bladder cancers per year counts only cases that newly developed.
expls.Cumulative incidence: That is wrong: cumulative incidence needs a group of fixed size followed over time, and men in several regions (estimated from census data) come and go, so a fixed-size denominator does not exist here.
expls.Complication rate: That is wrong: a complication rate describes untoward events in patients who already have a condition or procedure, whereas this denominator is all men at risk in the regions and the events are first diagnoses, which makes it an incidence measure.

2.2.guide_fact: A prevalence (cross-sectional) study assesses a sample of a defined population for the presence of a condition at one point in time, so it involves no follow-up period.

2.4.guide_fact: When incidence and prevalence are stable, average duration of disease equals prevalence divided by incidence, so a prevalence of 1.5% with an incidence of 50 per 100,000 per year gives 30 years.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 18
3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

expls.15: Dividing 1.5% by 50 per 100,000 per year (0.015 / 0.0005) gives 30, not 15. A duration of 15 years would need a prevalence of only 0.75% at the same incidence.
expls.25: The ratio 0.015 / 0.0005 is 30 years, not 25. A duration of 25 years would need a prevalence of 1.25% at this incidence, which is not what the studies show.
expls.30: Correct. In a steady state, prevalence equals incidence times average duration, so duration = prevalence / incidence = 0.015 / (50 / 100,000 per year) = 30 years.
expls.33: That is wrong: 33 years would need a prevalence of about 1.65% at this incidence. The correct ratio 0.015 / 0.0005 is exactly 30, and 33 does not come from a valid rearrangement of these numbers.
expls.50: That is wrong: 50 is simply the incidence figure (per 100,000 per year) copied as the answer. A 50-year duration would need a prevalence of 2.5%, and the actual ratio of 1.5% to 0.05% per year is 30 years.

2.5.guide_fact: A cohort is a group with a common characteristic assembled at a similar point and followed forward over time; reviewing the earlier course of patients who are already under care, with no common starting point, is not a cohort study.

expls.The proportion of patients with stomach: This is a cohort study, so it is not the answer: patients with stomach cancer form a group with a shared characteristic (the disease) who are followed forward in time to see how many are alive at 5 years.
expls.The risk of developing diabetes mellitus: This is a cohort study, so it is not the answer: children grouped by weight (the exposure) and followed forward for the development of diabetes is the classic exposure-defined cohort design.
expls.Complications of influenza vaccine among: This is a cohort study, so it is not the answer: children vaccinated in 2011 share a characteristic (receiving an intervention at a similar time) and are followed forward for complications.
expls.The earlier course of disease in a group: Correct. A cohort is a group with a common characteristic assembled at a similar point, such as disease onset, and followed forward; patients already under care at varied stages, whose earlier course is reviewed, share no common starting point, so this is not a cohort study.
expls.Patients admitted to an intensive care u: This is a cohort study, so it is not the answer: admission to the intensive care unit is the shared starting point, and the patients are followed forward to the outcome of being alive at discharge.

2.5.correct: The earlier course of disease in a group of patients now under care in a clinic

2.6.guide_fact: A sample chosen by a convenient rule with no random element, such as enrolling every 10th admitted patient with no random start, is a convenience sample and may misrepresent the population.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

expls.Stratified sample: That is wrong: a stratified sample first divides the population into subgroups (such as age or ethnicity) and samples within each, but here there are no subgroups, only a fixed rule based on admission order.
expls.Probability sample: That is wrong: a probability sample requires that each patient have a known chance of selection set by a chance process, and this design describes no random start or other chance mechanism, only a convenient rule tied to the order of arrival.
expls.Convenience sample: Correct, as the best of these choices. Enrolling every 10th admission is a convenient rule with no stated random element or random start (strictly this is systematic sampling, which counts as a probability sample only when the starting point is chosen at random); it might produce a representative sample, but because selection is not by chance it could misrepresent the hospital's patients.
expls.Random sample: That is wrong: in a random sample every patient has an equal chance of being selected by chance, but here selection is fixed by position in the admission order with no random element, so it is not random even if the resulting sample looks representative.
expls.Oversample: That is wrong: an oversample deliberately takes extra people from a subgroup to study it, and nothing in this design targets a subgroup; it is a fixed every-10th rule.

2.6.conflict: Keyed answer kept. Systematic sampling (every 10th) with a randomly chosen starting point is often treated as a probability sample; the stem gives no random start or chance mechanism, so convenience sample is the best of the listed choices, but the item is debatable.

2.7.guide_fact: Point prevalence is measured at a single point in time for each person, and that point need not be the same calendar date for everyone in the study.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15

expls.Point prevalence: Correct. Each patient was assessed at a single point in time (one survey day at each hospital), and the proportion with an infection on that day is point prevalence; the survey dates may differ between hospitals.
expls.Complication rate: That is wrong: a complication rate describes untoward events among patients who already have a condition or procedure, whereas this is the share of all sampled patients found to have an infection on the survey day.
expls.Incidence density: That is wrong: incidence density counts new cases over person-time in a changing population, but this survey followed no one over time and counted every infection present on the survey day, not only new ones.
expls.Cumulative incidence: That is wrong: cumulative incidence follows a fixed-size group forward and counts new cases, but here each patient was seen once on a single day with no follow-up.
expls.Period prevalence: That is wrong: period prevalence counts cases present at any time during a defined span, but each person was assessed at only one time point; the four-month spread only reflects that hospitals were surveyed on different dates.

2.8.guide_fact: Cumulative incidence is the proportion of a fixed-size group (a cohort) that develops the outcome over a period, such as children with a first seizure who have another during childhood.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17
3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 25

expls.Point prevalence: That is wrong: point prevalence is a snapshot of existing cases at one time, but this one-in-three figure comes from following children forward and counting who has a new seizure.
expls.Cumulative incidence: Correct. The children start as a fixed-size cohort with a first seizure and are followed forward, and the proportion who develop a new event (another seizure) over time is cumulative incidence.
expls.Complication rate: That is wrong: a complication rate describes untoward events in patients undergoing a treatment or procedure, while this is the risk of a repeat event in a fixed cohort followed through childhood, which is cumulative incidence.
expls.Period prevalence: That is wrong: period prevalence counts all existing cases during a span of time in a population, but here a fixed cohort was followed forward to count new recurrences.
expls.Incidence density: That is wrong: incidence density has a person-time denominator for a changing population, whereas this cohort is a fixed group of children with a first seizure and the figure is a simple proportion.

6.12.guide_fact: Stratification controls confounding by comparing rates within subgroups with otherwise similar probability of the outcome, such as aspirin users and non-users who have similar indications for the drug.

expls.Calculate the absolute risk of cardiovas: This does not remove the problem: absolute risk and the risk difference are just incidence and attributable risk from the crude comparison, so they still mix in the fact that sicker people chose aspirin; describing risk is not a way of controlling confounding.

7.1.guide_fact: In a case-control study, exposure information can be artificially higher in cases because of recall bias and more careful questioning, recording, or abstraction, which falsely raises the odds ratio; an exposure recorded only after the disease began cannot be a cause of it.

expls.Physicians might have asked about use of: This could bias the study toward an association: if physicians questioned cases more carefully about pill use, exposure would be found more often in cases than in controls, which inflates the odds ratio.
expls.Having a myocardial infarction might hav: Correct. This is the exception. Pill use abstracted from records at the time of the infarction reflects use that came before the event, so the infarction cannot have led to it and creates no false excess of exposure in cases. The other statements each describe exposure being asked about, recorded, abstracted, or recalled more readily in cases, which falsely raises the odds ratio.
expls.Physicians might have been more likely t: This could bias the study toward an association: if physicians recorded pill use more often for cases, exposure looks more frequent in cases than it truly was, which falsely raises the odds ratio.
expls.Medical record abstractors might have lo: This could bias the study toward an association: abstractors who know a patient had a myocardial infarction may search harder for pill use, so exposure is found more often in cases and the odds ratio is falsely elevated.
expls.Patients might have recalled exposure mo: This is recall bias: subjects asked about past exposure may remember it better once they have the disease being studied, so cases report exposure more readily than controls and the association is exaggerated.

7.1.correct: Having a myocardial infarction might have led to oral contraceptive use.

7.2.guide_fact: A case-control study, even a well-designed nested one, can show an association and identify a risk factor but cannot by itself establish cause, because risk factors may predict disease without causing it and unmeasured confounding is always possible.

expls.Vitamin D deficiency was a cause of colo: Correct. A case-control study, even a well-designed one nested in a cohort, cannot claim to have identified a cause: unmeasured confounding is always possible, and risk factors may predict disease without causing it (they may be disease markers).
expls.Vitamin D levels were associated with co: This can be said: lower vitamin D levels were found more often in patients with colon cancer, and an association is exactly what a case-control comparison of exposure between cases and controls measures.
expls.Vitamin D deficiency was a risk factor f: This can be said: vitamin D was measured years before diagnosis, so the low level came before the cancer, and a factor linked to a higher probability of developing disease later fits the definition of a risk factor.
expls.Nesting the study in a large cohort was: This can be said: sampling controls from the same large cohort as the cases gives a source population that is clearly defined, and exposure was measured in stored blood before diagnosis rather than recalled, which is a strength.
expls.The results might have been confounded w: This can be said: adjusting for measured confounders cannot remove the effect of confounders that were never measured, so the results might still be confounded by unmeasured variables related to both vitamin D and cancer.

7.2.correct: Vitamin D deficiency was a cause of colorectal cancer.

7.3.guide_fact: The odds ratio (relative odds) is the measure of association for case-control studies, whereas relative risk is used for cohort studies.

expls.Prevalence: Prevalence is the portion of a group with a condition at one point in time, usually found from a survey or cross-sectional study; a case-control study starts from chosen cases and controls, so it cannot give it.
expls.Odds ratio: Correct. The odds ratio (relative odds) is the measure of association for case-control studies, calculated as the odds of exposure in cases divided by the odds of exposure in controls, which equals ad over bc; it serves as an estimated relative risk.
expls.Risk difference: A risk difference (attributable risk) is the incidence in exposed persons minus the incidence in unexposed persons, so it needs incidence, which a case-control study cannot supply because the numbers of cases and controls are chosen by the investigator.
expls.Relative risk: Relative risk is the ratio of incidence in exposed to incidence in unexposed persons and is the measure for cohort studies; a case-control study yields the odds ratio instead, which only estimates relative risk.
expls.Incidence: Incidence, the number of new cases over a given time in a group, is established directly by cohort studies; a case-control study begins with cases and controls already selected, so it cannot report incidence.

7.4.guide_fact: An epidemic curve is the number of cases plotted against time (by date of onset of illness), showing the rise and fall of cases during an outbreak.

expls.The usual incubation period for the caus: The usual incubation period is a property of the organism, not what an epidemic curve shows; the curve plots cases against time of onset, and only its shape may hint at the interval between exposure and illness.
expls.A comparison of illness over time in exp: An epidemic curve does not compare exposed with nonexposed people; that comparison is made with attack rates or a cohort or case-control analysis. The curve plots only the number of cases over time.
expls.The onset of illness in cases over time: Correct. An epidemic (epi) curve is the number of cases plotted against time, usually by date of onset of illness, so it shows the rise and fall of cases over the course of the outbreak, as in the Legionnaires' disease outbreak plotted by date of onset.
expls.The duration of illness, on average, in: The curve marks when illness began in each case, not how long each person stayed ill, so it does not give the average duration of illness; duration would need recovery dates.
expls.The distribution of time from infection: The distribution of time from infection to first symptoms is the incubation period distribution; an epidemic curve counts cases by onset date and does not record each person's time of infection.

7.4.correct: The onset of illness in cases over time

7.5.guide_fact: Doing a case-control analysis within a cohort study is a more efficient way to control for confounders missing from the cohort dataset, because the extra data are collected only for cases and controls rather than the whole cohort.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15

expls.Case-control studies are a feasible way: Correct. If the cohort data lack variables that should be controlled for, a case-control analysis within the cohort is more efficient because the extra data need to be collected only for the cases and a sample of controls, not for the entire cohort.
expls.Case-control studies can provide all the: A case-control study cannot provide all the same information: it gives an odds ratio (an estimate of relative risk) but cannot establish incidence, which a cohort study measures directly.
expls.Case-control studies can determine incid: Incidence in exposed and nonexposed members is calculated directly from the whole cohort; a case-control study, which samples cases and controls, cannot determine incidence, so it is not the reason for this analysis.
expls.Case-control studies are in general stro: Case-control studies are not in general stronger than cohort studies; they are a step earlier in the usual study sequence and are limited by recall bias and dependence on choosing controls. Their advantage here is efficiency.

7.5.correct: Case-control studies are a feasible way of controlling for confounders not found in the cohort dataset.

7.6.guide_fact: It is best to obtain cases (and controls) from a cohort representative of the population rather than a dynamic population, especially if exposure or disease is changing rapidly over time.

expls.A sample from the general (dynamic) popu: A sample from a dynamic population is less good because exposure or disease may be changing over time, and controls may not be matched to the date each case developed disease. A defined cohort avoids these problems.
expls.Primary care physicians' offices: Primary care offices capture only people who present there, who may differ from the population that produced the cases, which invites selection bias; sampling from a cohort gives cases from a clearly defined source.
expls.A community: A community is a looser source than a cohort: the group is not clearly defined and followed, so it is harder to be sure cases and controls come from the same source population.
expls.A cohort representative of the populatio: Correct. Sampling cases (and controls) from a cohort representative of the population is best, especially when exposure or disease changes rapidly over time or when controls are not matched to the date of disease onset in cases.
expls.A hospital: Hospital patients are a convenient source but may differ systematically from everyone who has the disease, which can create selection bias; a cohort representative of the population is the better source.

7.6.correct: A cohort representative of the population

7.7.guide_fact: Multiple control groups are used to check whether the results are sensitive to the type of control group chosen, because the main control group may differ systematically from cases in ways other than the exposure of interest.

expls.To obtain a stronger estimate of relativ: Multiple control groups do not strengthen the estimate of relative risk; they test whether the odds ratio is robust, or sensitive, to the type of control group chosen.
expls.There are a limited number of cases and: Having few cases and many potential controls is the reason to use several controls per case, which adds statistical power. That is different from using multiple control groups of different types.
expls.To control for confounding: Confounding is controlled by matching, stratification, or adjustment; adding another control group does not remove a confounder, though it may reveal that the results depend on the controls chosen.
expls.To increase the generalizability of the: Generalizability depends on how representative the sampled cases and controls are of the wider population; adding control groups does not by itself broaden that.
expls.The main control group may be systematic: Correct. The main control group may differ from the cases in ways other than the exposure of interest; using a second control group shows whether results change substantially, and if they do the findings are called into question.

7.7.correct: The main control group may be systematically different from cases (other than on the exposure of interest)

expls.They crude odds ratio provides a good ap: Not here: the odds ratio approximates relative risk well only when the disease is rare, and in this registry 2,000 of 10,000 children (20%) developed celiac disease, which is common. expls.The crude odds ratio will overestimate r: Correct. expls.The control selection will provide a dir: Controls drawn only from children who stayed disease-free do not represent the exposure of the whole registry, which includes the 20% who developed disease; population-based sampling of noncases throughout the study would be needed for that.

7.9.guide_fact: Case-control studies do not provide information on incidence; a cohort study establishes incidence directly.

expls.The early symptoms of stomach cancer: A case-control study can do this: it compares people with stomach cancer with people without it, looking back at symptoms and other features that came earlier in the cases.
expls.Risk factors for sudden infant death syn: A case-control study can do this: sudden infant death syndrome is rare, and case-control studies are better than cohorts for rare disease because they need small samples and no waiting for the condition to develop.
expls.The incidence of suicide in the adult po: Correct. Incidence is the number of new cases over time in a population of known size; case-control studies choose their cases and controls, so they cannot provide incidence (a cohort study establishes incidence directly).
expls.The protective effect of aspirin: A case-control study can do this: if aspirin protects, it will be less common among cases than controls, giving an odds ratio below 1, which indicates a possible protective association.
expls.Modes of transmission of an infectious d: A case-control study can do this: comparing infected people with uninfected people for exposures such as foods or contacts shows how the disease is being spread, which is a common use in outbreaks.

7.10.guide_fact: Matching selects controls with the same characteristics as cases on a few major variables (other than the exposure under study), so that cases and controls at least do not differ on those variables.

expls.To control for all potential confounding: Matching controls only the few variables that are matched. Other confounders, including unmeasured ones, are handled by other methods such as stratification or adjustment in the analysis.
expls.To make cases and controls similar to ea: Correct. expls.To make it possible to examine the effec: Matching makes cases and controls equal on the matched variables, so it removes the differences needed to study their effects; the effect of a matched variable on the estimated relative risk cannot be examined.
expls.To test whether the right controls were: Testing whether the right controls were chosen is the job of a second, different control group; matching does not test control selection but builds similarity into it.
expls.To increase the generalizability of the: Matching does not improve generalizability; it forces controls to resemble the cases, which if anything ties the comparison to that type of person rather than broadening the population the results apply to.

7.11.guide_fact: The odds ratio is ad / bc: with 60 of 100 cases and 40 of 100 controls exposed, it is (60 x 60) / (40 x 40) = 2.25.

expls.0.44: 0.44 is the reciprocal of the correct value (40 x 40 divided by 60 x 60): the cases' exposure odds were put on the bottom instead of the top. That would make the exposure look protective when it was more common in cases.

expls.Not possible to calculate: The odds ratio can be calculated: the numbers of exposed and unexposed cases (60 and 40) and controls (40 and 60) fill every cell of the 2 x 2 table, and that is all the odds ratio requires.

expls.The population attributable risk of dise: Population attributable risk depends on the incidence of disease in the population, and case-control studies cannot supply incidence because cases and controls are selected by the investigator.
expls.Multiple outcomes (diseases): A case-control study begins with one outcome (disease or no disease) and looks back at exposures. Studying multiple outcomes is an advantage of cohort studies, which follow an exposure forward.
expls.The incidence of rare diseases: Case-control studies are well suited to rare disease, but they cannot report incidence, since the number of cases and controls is set by the investigator; incidence is established directly by cohort studies.
expls.The prevalence of disease: Prevalence, the portion of a group with a condition at a point in time, comes from cross-sectional (prevalence) studies of a population, not from a case-control study.
expls.Risk factors for disease: Correct. A case-control study compares people with and without one disease for earlier exposure, so it is useful for identifying risk factors for that disease, giving an odds ratio that estimates relative risk.

7.16.guide_fact: Sampling cases and controls from a defined population or cohort tends to give cases and controls that are representative of the source population.

8.1.guide_fact: In a prognosis study, all members of the cohort are identified at a similar point in the course of disease, called zero time, such as the diagnosis of the condition that defines the cohort, and not at the time of the outcome.

8.2.guide_fact: Migration bias occurs when patients drop out of a cohort study, and it distorts results only if the dropouts differ in prognosis from those who remain; the more dropouts, the greater the potential for bias.

expls.When in the course of follow-up the chil: The timing of leaving can change how much follow-up each child contributes, but it does not by itself distort the comparison. What matters most is whether the children who left had a different prognosis from those who stayed.
expls.Whether dropping out was related to prog: Correct. Migration bias arises when patients drop out and those who leave are not similar to those who stay. expls.Whether the number of children dropping: Similar numbers of dropouts in the two groups do not protect the results. expls.Rates of incontinence were higher in the: Correct. A higher rate of incontinence in men who had surgery is the study result, and it can reflect a true effect of surgery. expls.Cohort study: A cohort study assembles a group at a similar point in the disease course and follows it over time to measure outcomes. expls.Case-control study: A case-control study defines groups by outcome (disease or no disease) and compares exposures between them. This study has no comparison group without the disease; it only describes a group of patients who have it.
expls.Case series: Correct. 8.6.guide_fact: In time-to-event analysis, a patient is censored when they are removed from the study or have not been followed for the full time period, and merely developing another disease that could be fatal does not cause censoring while the patient is still alive and under observation.

expls.The patient died of another cause before: This patient can be censored. Someone who dies of a cause unrelated to the outcome being followed leaves observation without having had the event of interest, so the patient is counted only for the time observed before that death.
expls.The patient decided not to continue in t: This patient is censored. A patient who decides to leave the study is no longer observed, so their survival after that point is unknown and they are counted only for the time they were followed.
expls.The patient had been enrolled in the stu: This patient is censored. Someone enrolled for less than 3 years has not yet been followed as long as the analysis time, so their survival to year 3 is unknown at analysis and they count only for the time observed.
expls.The patient developed another disease th: Correct. Developing another potentially fatal disease does not remove anyone from observation. Patients are censored when they leave the study or have not been followed for the full period; a patient who has another disease but is still alive and being followed remains in the analysis.

If the event were death from any cause, that death would be the event itself. The keyed answer still stands because developing another disease without dying never removes a patient from observation.

8.7.guide_fact: Prognosis concerns outcomes of disease over time, and a prevalence (cross-sectional) study measures a condition at a single point in time and does not measure events over time, so it cannot identify prognostic factors.

expls.Prevalence study: Correct. A prevalence study assesses a population for a condition at one point in time, so it measures no events over time. Prognosis is about outcomes of disease over time, so this design cannot identify prognostic factors (prevalence studies are also poor for cause and effect and better for developing hypotheses).
expls.Time-to-event analysis: Time-to-event analysis can identify prognostic factors. Cox proportional hazards regression can find prognostic indicators of survival in a given disease, taking into account the effects of several predictors on the survival curve.
expls.Case-control study: A case-control study can be used to look for prognostic factors, because patients who had the outcome can be compared with patients who did not for earlier characteristics. It is not the design that fails; the prevalence study is, since it measures no events over time.
expls.Cohort study: A cohort study can identify prognostic factors. Patients are followed over time from zero time, and the factors present at the start are compared between those who do and do not develop the outcome.

8.8.guide_fact: A survival curve gives the estimated probability of surviving to any point in time from zero time, calculated from the cumulative probability of surviving each preceding interval, and it estimates survival for a hypothetical rather than an actual cohort.

expls.An unbiased estimate of survival even if: A survival curve does not guarantee an unbiased estimate. Patients who leave the study (migration) can bias the curve if they differ from those who stay, and the more dropouts, the greater the potential for bias.
expls.The estimated probability of survival fr: Correct. A survival curve gives the estimated probability of surviving to any point in time, calculated from the cumulative probability of surviving each preceding interval, starting at zero time. It estimates survival for a hypothetical rather than an actual cohort.
expls.The proportion of a cohort still alive a: The curve does not simply report the proportion of the original cohort alive at the end of follow-up. It is an estimate built interval by interval that accounts for patients who left the study, and it shows survival at every point in time rather than only at the end.
expls.The rate at which original members of th: The curve shows deaths (events) over time, not how fast members leave the study. Patients who leave are taken into account in the estimate, but their departure rate is not what is plotted.
expls.The cumulative survival of a cohort over: A survival curve does track survival cumulatively, so this is close, but it is not the best description. The curve gives the estimated probability of surviving from zero time, built interval by interval and adjusted for patients who left, and it estimates survival for a hypothetical rather than an actual cohort, so it is not a direct count of the actual cohort's survivors.

8.8.correct: The estimated probability of survival from zero time

8.9.guide_fact: The most appropriate sample for a prognosis study depends on who will use the results, because the referral pattern of the patients affects whether the findings apply to a given clinician's patients.

expls.Members of the general population: The general population is mostly people who do not have the disease, whereas prognosis studies follow people who already have it, so this sample does not describe the course of illness for a specific group of patients. The best sample depends on who will use the results.
expls.Patients in primary care in the communit: Patients in primary care are right if the results will be used by primary care clinicians, but this sample would not describe the prognosis of patients seen at specialist centers, so it is not always the most appropriate.
expls.Patients admitted to a community hospita: Patients admitted to a community hospital represent one referral pattern and one setting. They fit users of that setting, but they may differ from patients in primary care or at referral centers, so this is not the best sample in every case.
expls.Patients referred to a specialist: Patients referred to a specialist are a selected group whose referral pattern differs from community care. They suit specialist users, but results from academic or referral centers may not apply to patients seen elsewhere.
expls.It depends on who will use the results o: Correct. The right sample depends on the question: referral pattern (academic medical center versus community) affects who is in the study, and results apply only to patients similar to those the reader sees. Prognosis in primary care and among those referred to specialists are both useful to know.

8.10.guide_fact: Generalizability is often limited because patients in a study, for example those who met rigorous trial entry criteria at referral centers, may not be representative of other populations or of individual patients.

expls.Inconsistent zero time: Zero time was consistent here. Patients were enrolled at the time of diagnosis, so all were counted from a similar point in the disease course, which is what an inception cohort requires.
expls.Generalizability: Correct. Patients had to meet stringent trial entry criteria at referral centers, so the usual-care patients are not representative of people with multiple sclerosis in the general population or in a defined clinical setting. Generalizability is often limited because study patients may not be representative of other populations.
expls.Measurement bias: Nothing in the study suggests measurement bias. All patients were examined yearly in the same way, so no group had a greater chance of outcome detection, and walking ability is a straightforward outcome.
expls.Migration bias: Migration bias is not the problem here. All patients remained under observation for 10 years, so no dropouts changed the composition of the cohort.
expls.Failure to use time-to-event methods: With every patient examined yearly and observed for the full 10 years, there were no incomplete-follow-up problems that time-to-event methods exist to handle. The main limitation is who was studied, not how the results were analyzed.

8.11.guide_fact: Multiple imputation estimates missing values by statistical modeling of patients with complete data, and it assumes that the measured characteristics can reliably predict the missing values.

expls.Multiple imputation assumes that the cha: Correct. Multiple imputation is a technique for estimating missing values by statistical modeling of the patients with complete data, taking their other characteristics into account. It therefore assumes that the measured characteristics can reliably predict what is missing.
expls.Multiple imputation removes the effects: Imputation does not remove the effects of bias. If patients who dropped out differ from those who stayed in ways that the measured characteristics do not capture, the estimates can still be biased.
expls.Multiple imputation can estimate headach: Imputation does not simply pick headache present or absent at random from patients with complete follow-up. It builds a statistical model from complete cases and other characteristics to estimate the missing values; a simple average of measured values is a cruder and likely biased approach.
expls.Complete case analysis compares the resu: Complete case analysis uses only patients with complete information and leaves out those with missing values; it does not compare the two groups. Excluding dropouts can bias results, which is why imputation is considered.

8.11.correct: Multiple imputation assumes that the characteristics measured in the study can be used to reliably estimate the missing values.

8.12.guide_fact: The strongest evidence for choosing a clinical prediction rule is that it has been shown to predict outcomes in patients other than those used to develop it, that is, validated in different settings.

expls.The prediction rule classifies patients: Separating patients into groups with very different prognosis is a desirable feature, but a rule can do this in the patients it was built on and still fail elsewhere. That is why testing in other patients matters more.
expls.The prediction rule has been validated i: Correct. Even a rule built with the best methods is most strongly tested by showing that it predicts outcomes in patients other than those used to develop it. Study patients must be similar to your own for a rule to apply, so validation in different settings is the most important reason.
The number of variables is not the measure of a good rule. Multiple factors predict better than a single data point, but including many variables does not show that the rule works in other patients.
expls.Prognostic factors include state-of-the-: Using state-of-the-science diagnostic tests does not show that a rule predicts well. Rules are more practical when they rely on readily available clinical data, and what demonstrates that a rule works is that it predicts outcomes in patients other than those used to develop it.
How the score is calculated is a convenience, not evidence of accuracy. A rule may be simple to compute by hand or by computer, but only testing in other patients shows whether it predicts well.

8.12.correct: The prediction rule has been validated in different settings.

8.13.guide_fact: A hazard ratio from a Cox proportional hazards survival analysis can be interpreted as a relative risk: a hazard ratio of 5 means the exposed group has five times the risk of the outcome compared with the unexposed group.

expls.In this study, it is the rate of continu: The hazard ratio here is not the ratio of the rates of smoking and quitting. It compares the rate of the outcome, amputation, in the two groups: patients who continued to smoke relative to those who quit.
expls.It can be estimated from a case-control: A case-control study measures exposure between cases and controls and yields an odds ratio. A hazard ratio comes from following patients over time in a survival analysis, which needs time-to-event information that a case-control study does not provide.
expls.It cannot be adjusted for the presence o: A hazard ratio can be adjusted. Cox proportional hazards regression studies the effect of an exposure on outcome after adjusting for confounders and for other factors related to prognosis.
expls.It conveys information similar to relati: Correct. The hazard ratio from a Cox survival analysis can be interpreted like a relative risk: a ratio of 5 means patients who continued to smoke have five times the risk of amputation compared with those who quit; a ratio below 1 would mean protection.
expls.It is calculated from the cumulative inc: A hazard ratio compares the rate at which the event occurs over time in the two groups, estimated with survival analysis, rather than dividing the proportions who had the outcome. 9.1.guide_fact: A pragmatic trial tests treatments under real, ordinary circumstances (broad eligibility, usual care, no special blinding, patient-centered outcomes), in contrast to an efficacy trial, which tests them under ideal circumstances.

expls.Pragmatic trial: Correct. This trial was built to mirror everyday practice: two drugs already in common use, broad eligibility, no blinding after enrollment, usual care for everything except the study drugs, and a patient-centered questionnaire outcome. That is a pragmatic trial, which asks whether a treatment works under ordinary circumstances.
expls.Large simple trial: A large simple trial needs a very large number of participants with minimal data collection, and this trial enrolled only three hundred patients. Its real-world design features make it pragmatic, not large.
expls.Efficacy trial: An efficacy trial tests a treatment under ideal circumstances, typically with narrow eligibility, tight control of care, and blinding. This trial deliberately did the opposite (broad eligibility, usual care, no blinding), so its results speak to effectiveness in ordinary circumstances.
expls.Equivalence trial: An equivalence trial is designed to show that two treatments have effects that are essentially the same. Nothing in this trial is built around proving sameness; its defining features concern how closely it resembles real-world care.
expls.Noninferiority trial: A noninferiority trial asks whether a new treatment is unlikely to be less effective than an established one, usually because the new one is cheaper, safer, or easier. Here both drugs are already in common use and no new-versus-established question is posed; the design features describe a pragmatic trial.

9.2.guide_fact: Intention-to-treat analysis counts outcomes by the group patients were randomized to, so it shows the effect of offering a treatment regardless of whether patients actually take it (effectiveness in ordinary circumstances).

expls.It describes the effects of treatments t: Describing the effects of treatments patients actually received is the opposite of intention-to-treat analysis, which counts patients in the group they were randomized to. Analysis by treatment actually received is a per-protocol or as-treated analysis, which is not protected by randomization.
expls.It is unlikely to underestimate treatmen: Intention-to-treat analysis does not protect against underestimating the effect. When patients assigned to a treatment do not take it, or cross over, the two groups become more alike and the measured difference shrinks toward no effect.
expls.It is not affected by patients dropping: Intention-to-treat analysis is affected by dropouts. Patients who stop treatment stay in their assigned group, which dilutes the observed difference. What intention-to-treat does is keep everyone in the analysis rather than dropping them.
expls.It describes the consequences of offerin: Correct. Patients are analyzed according to the group they were randomized to, so the result shows the consequences of offering a treatment, whether or not patients take it. This reflects effectiveness in ordinary circumstances, where compliance is imperfect.
expls.It describes whether treatment can work: Effects under ideal circumstances describe efficacy, where everyone takes the treatment as intended. Intention-to-treat analysis includes the noncompliance and dropouts of real life, so it addresses effectiveness rather than efficacy.

9.3.guide_fact: Only characteristics that exist at the time of randomization (such as disease severity) are randomly allocated, so subgroup comparisons on those characteristics remain randomized; characteristics arising afterward (retention, response, compliance) are not.

expls.The subset of patients who, at the time: Correct. expls.Patients who experienced other treatment: Whether patients experienced other treatments is decided after randomization by clinicians and patients, not by chance. Groups formed this way can differ in prognosis for reasons unrelated to the drug, so this is an observational comparison subject to confounding.
expls.Patients who remained in the trial versu: Staying in the trial or dropping out happens after randomization and is related to how patients are doing and to side effects. The two groups formed by retention differ in more than chance, so this is not a randomized comparison.

expls.Patients who took the drug compared with: Taking the drug (compliance) is a behavior that arises after randomization, and patients who take medication often differ from those who do not in health, motivation, and other prognostic factors. expls.Reported effects are for patients who ha: This is a genuine advantage of observational studies. expls.It may be possible to carry out these st: This is a genuine advantage of observational studies. They can be done with records and data already collected for other purposes, which avoids the cost and logistics of enrolling, randomizing, and following participants prospectively.

Strict inclusion and exclusion criteria (and a compliance run-in) make trial patients more alike and more likely to follow the program, so a real difference between treatments is easier to detect. 9.6.guide_fact: Intention-to-treat analysis compares the effects of being offered treatments (a randomized comparison relevant to effectiveness); it does not describe the effects of actually taking treatment.

9.7.guide_fact: Stratified randomization (randomizing separately within strata of a baseline variable) is particularly helpful when that variable is strongly related to prognosis, especially in smaller trials where chance imbalance is a concern.

9.8.guide_fact: In a per-protocol analysis, outcomes are attributed to the treatment patients actually received rather than the group they were randomized to, which is what an intention-to-treat analysis uses.

expls.Superiority: Superiority describes the goal of a trial, which is to determine whether one treatment is better than another. It says nothing about whether patients are analyzed by treatment received or by assigned group.
expls.Intention-to-treat: Intention-to-treat analysis is the opposite approach: patients are analyzed in the group they were randomized to, regardless of the treatment they actually received.
expls.Noninferiority: Noninferiority describes a trial goal, which is to show that a new treatment is not unacceptably worse than an established one. It is not a way of assigning outcomes to treatment groups.
expls.Open label: Open label means no blinding is done, so participants and investigators know the treatment. It describes knowledge of treatment assignment, not how outcomes are attributed in the analysis.
expls.Per-protocol: Correct. In a per-protocol analysis, outcomes are attributed to the treatment patients actually received rather than the group they were randomized to. Because who takes treatment is no longer random, it loses randomization's protection against confounding.

9.9.guide_fact: Side effects such as a slower pulse and lethargy can reveal who is taking the active drug to patients, to physicians, and to anyone who observes patients after treatment starts, but they cannot affect allocation concealment, because assignment is made before treatment begins.

expls.The patients' physicians: Physicians caring for patients would notice the lower pulse rate and lethargy that the beta-blocker causes, which reveals who is taking the active drug. Even when blinded at the start, treatment effects and side effects can unmask the treatment group.

The investigators who assign patients to groups make that decision before any drug is started, so no side effect can reveal the assignment to them. This is allocation concealment, in which the people assigning patients are kept unaware of which treatment comes next.

9.10.guide_fact: Randomization is ethical when there is no conclusive evidence that one of the treatments is better than the other (the state called equipoise).

expls.The drugs are known to be equally effect: If the drugs were known to be equally effective, there would be conclusive evidence about the comparison and nothing left to test. Equipoise means genuine uncertainty about which is better, not knowledge that they are the same.

Either way, the choice does not describe the state of uncertainty that justifies a trial.

Equipoise means the scientific community has no conclusive evidence that either drug is better; there may be opinions and partial evidence, but no consensus. Randomization is ethical only in this state of uncertainty, and the trial is done to resolve it.
expls.Although one drug is more effective, the: If one drug were known to be more effective, patients randomized to the other would be denied a treatment known to work better. That is conclusive evidence about efficacy, so this is not equipoise, even though the other drug's convenience and side effects may matter.

9.10.correct: Neither drug is known to be more effective than the other.

9.11.guide_fact: A noninferiority trial determines whether a new treatment is unlikely to be less effective than an established treatment when the new treatment has other advantages such as lower cost or fewer side effects.
cites: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

expls.Superiority: A superiority trial tries to show that one treatment is better than another. Antibiotic B is cheaper and has fewer side effects, and the goal is to show it is not worse, so the question is not whether B is better in efficacy.
expls.Crossover: Crossover refers to participants moving from one randomly assigned treatment to another. It describes how patients move between treatments, not the question of whether a new drug is no worse than the established drug.
expls.Cluster: Cluster refers to selecting or assigning whole groups (for example hospital units) instead of individual patients. It concerns how participants are grouped and does not address whether antibiotic B is no less effective than A.
expls.Noninferiority: Correct. A noninferiority trial determines whether a new treatment is unlikely to be less effective than an established one. It fits antibiotic B, which has advantages (cheaper, fewer side effects) but whose efficacy relative to antibiotic A is not established. It usually needs a larger sample size than a superiority trial because differences may be small.
expls.Equivalence: An equivalence trial aims to show the two drugs are essentially the same in both directions. For antibiotic B, the important question is whether it is no worse than A, since better or equal efficacy plus lower cost and fewer side effects would be acceptable, which is the noninferiority question.

9.12.guide_fact: Making the primary outcome a composite of clinically important, related outcomes increases the number of outcome events and therefore the trial's ability to detect an effect if one is present.

expls.There are more outcomes events than ther: Correct. Combining related, clinically important outcomes produces more outcome events than any single outcome would, which increases the trial's ability to detect a real effect if one exists. The drawback is that the intervention may affect components differently, and the composite can mask this.
expls.All outcomes are equally affected by the: The interventions may affect the components differently; one outcome may improve while another does not or worsens. That is the main disadvantage of a composite, which can hide differing effects, so it is not an advantage.
Combining outcomes does not affect generalizability, which depends on how representative the patients and setting are. A composite outcome changes the number of events, not who is studied.
expls.Each of the individual outcomes is impor: Each component having clinical importance is a requirement for a sensible composite, so that the combination is meaningful. It is not the advantage of combining them; the advantage is the larger total number of events.
expls.If one outcome is infrequent, others mak: This misstates the benefit. Pooling outcomes adds up events to give the trial more power, but a frequent outcome does not substitute for an infrequent one in interpretation: the composite can hide that individual components respond differently, so the infrequent outcome's own effect remains unknown.

9.12.conflict: Keyed answer kept. The last option (other outcomes make up for an infrequent one) overlaps with the keyed statement; the key states the advantage directly (more total events, more ability to detect an effect).

9.13.guide_fact: Baseline differences between randomized groups can result from chance (bad luck in randomization) or from a breakdown in allocation concealment, and small differences are expected.

expls.“Bad luck” in randomization: Chance can produce imbalance between randomly allocated groups, especially in smaller trials, so this is a possible explanation. But it is not the only one, since a breakdown in allocation concealment can also produce imbalanced groups.
expls.A breakdown in allocation concealment: A breakdown in allocation concealment (by poor methods or cheating) lets those assigning patients steer them into groups, which would show up as baseline differences, so it is a possible explanation. expls.Both: Correct. Bad luck in randomization and a breakdown in allocation concealment can each leave baseline characteristics different between the groups. Small differences are expected by chance; the challenge is deciding how large a difference must be to raise concern.

9.14.guide_fact: Phase III trials are larger randomized trials that give definitive evidence of efficacy or effectiveness (and some common side effects), but usually do not identify uncommon side effects.

expls.The relationship between dose and effica: The relationship between dose and efficacy is examined in Phase II trials, which involve a small number of participants and identify preliminary effect and any relationship to dose. Phase III trials aim at definitive evidence of effect.
expls.Rates of uncommon side effects: Uncommon side effects are usually not identified in Phase III trials. They are detected by postmarketing surveillance, which follows large numbers of patients after the drug is released.
expls.Efficacy or effectiveness: Correct. Phase III trials are larger, randomized trials intended to give definitive evidence of efficacy or effectiveness and identify some common side effects. These are the trials usually published in the clinical literature.
expls.The dose range that is well tolerated: The dose range that is well tolerated is worked out in Phase I trials, which use a small number of participants without a control group to identify a safe, tolerated dose.

9.15.guide_fact: The main advantage of randomized controlled trials over observational studies of treatment effects is prevention of confounding, which is why they are the gold standard for evaluating treatment efficacy.

expls.Fewer ethical challenges: Randomized controlled trials have more ethical challenges, not fewer, because investigators assign treatments by chance. That is acceptable only with genuine uncertainty about which treatment is better, with participant consent, and with stopping the study if harm, futility, or benefit becomes evident.
expls.Prevention of confounding: Correct. Randomization creates groups that would have the same outcome rates, on average, were it not for the treatment, so confounding is prevented. In observational studies, systematic differences in groups other than the treatment factor make confounding difficult to avoid; this is why randomized trials are the gold standard for treatment efficacy.
expls.Resemble usual care: Whether a trial resembles usual care depends on its design; observational studies of patients currently being treated are the ones that naturally reflect real-world care. It is not an inherent advantage of randomized trials.
expls.Quicker answer: Randomized controlled trials are not quicker; they involve logistical issues such as sample selection, randomization, blinding, consistency across participants, and time. An observational study using existing data can often give an answer sooner.
expls.Less expensive: Randomized controlled trials are more expensive, not less, because of the logistics of recruiting, randomizing, blinding, and following participants. Their cost is accepted because of what they prevent, which is confounding.

10.1.guide_fact: The relative risk reduction is the absolute risk reduction divided by the risk in the control group, which equals 1 minus the relative risk; here (0.0079 - 0.0053)/0.0079 is about 33%.

expls.385: Correct. The number needed to screen is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction: the difference in death risk is 0.0079 - 0.0053 = 0.0026, and 1/0.0026 is about 385 people screened over 13 years to prevent one death from colorectal cancer. 10.3.guide_fact: Higher sensitivity lowers the negative likelihood ratio (0.20 to 0.11 here), so the probability of disease after a negative test decreases, while lower specificity adds false positives and lowers the positive predictive value.
