10.5.guide_fact: Lead time is the time between detection by screening and when the condition would have been diagnosed from symptoms, so apparent survival improves without any improvement in death.

expls.Lead-time bias: Correct. Lead time is the interval between detection by screening and when the cancer would have been diagnosed from symptoms. expls.Length-time bias: Length-time bias arises because screening preferentially finds slow-growing, better-prognosis cancers. It can contribute, but it is not the best single explanation here: the best-fit explanation is that earlier diagnosis simply lengthened the time from diagnosis to death (lead time).

expls.There were more smokers in the screened: Randomization spreads smoking and other risk factors about evenly between the groups, so a chance excess of smokers is an unlikely reason for 206 versus 160 cancers in a trial of about 9,000 men.

expls.Screening picked up some cancers that wo: Correct. Overdiagnosis means detecting disease that would never have caused symptoms or needed treatment. expls.Overdiagnosis is not present because the: This statement is false. 10.8.guide_fact: A test with a higher false-positive rate has lower specificity and, at a given prevalence, a lower positive predictive value, because positive predictive value is true positives divided by all positive results.

10.9.guide_fact: When judging a vaccine, efficacy, safety and the burden of the disease matter most, and cost is only one component of a cost-effectiveness analysis.

expls.Efficacy in preventing the disease: Efficacy is central: a vaccine that does not prevent the disease has no purpose. Efficacy asks whether it works under ideal conditions, and effectiveness asks whether it works in everyday practice; both are essential.
expls.Safety of the vaccine: Safety is central: giving a vaccine to healthy people is only justified if harms are small, and adverse effects are studied with longitudinal follow-up. Safety is always weighed against benefit.
expls.Danger of the disease: The danger of the disease (burden of suffering, such as mortality and hospitalizations) is a core reason to include a condition in preventive care. A mild or rare disease may not justify a vaccine.

expls.Volunteers tend to be more interested in: Correct. This is compliance bias: people who volunteer for screening are more invested in their health and more compliant with advice, so they do better regardless of the test. expls.People who refuse screening are usually: This is backward. There is no reason refusers would be healthier; the pattern reported is that those who decline preventive care tend to have worse outcomes, and health-seeking behavior is what separates the groups.
expls.Volunteers for screening are more likely: Greater need for screening would predict worse outcomes in volunteers, not the better outcomes reported here. expls.When a screening program is begun, more: This statement is true, so it is not the exception. The first round of screening detects prevalent cases (everyone with existing disease), while later rounds detect mainly incident (new) cases, so the yield is highest at the start.

expls.Medical costs, such as those associated: This is true but incomplete. The cost of delivering the preventive activity is one part, but a cost-effectiveness analysis must also include other medical costs (follow-up of positive tests and treatment) and indirect costs.
expls.All medical costs, including diagnostic: This is true but incomplete. Diagnostic follow-up and treatment costs, with and without prevention, belong in the analysis, but lost income and other indirect costs must also be counted.
expls.Indirect costs, such as loss of income d: This is true but incomplete. Lost income from time off work is a real cost of both prevention and disease, but it is only one category; medical costs of delivering, following up and treating must also be included.

expls.All of the above: Correct. A cost-effectiveness analysis takes a societal perspective and captures all costs: delivery of the preventive activity, diagnostic follow-up and treatment (with and without prevention), and indirect costs for patients and caregivers. Costs without prevention are subtracted from costs with prevention to estimate the cost per health effect.

11.2.guide_fact: The P value is the probability that a difference as big as or bigger than the one observed could have arisen by chance alone; P = 0.001 means 1 chance in 1,000.

expls.Bias is unlikely to account for the obse: The P value addresses only chance (random error). Bias, such as measurement bias or selection bias, is a separate systematic problem, and a very small P value says nothing about whether it is present.
A P value cannot show clinical importance. A 2 mg/dL difference on a cholesterol of about 240 mg/dL (under 1 percent) is far too small to matter to patients, yet with 10,000 patients it can still be very highly statistically significant.
expls.A difference as big as or bigger than wh: Correct. The P value is the probability of seeing a difference this large or larger by chance alone; P < 0.001 means that chance would produce it less than 1 time in 1,000. It says nothing about bias, importance, or generalizability.
expls.The results are generalizable to other p: The P value does not speak to generalizability, meaning whether results apply to other settings or patients. This trial studied hyperlipidemia, so patients with a different condition such as hypertension are outside what it tested.
expls.The statistical power of this study was: Power is about the chance of missing a real difference (a false-negative result). This trial found a highly significant difference, so a missed effect is not the issue, and the P value itself does not measure power.

11.2.correct: A difference as big as or bigger than what was observed could have arisen by chance less than one time in 1,000.

11.3.guide_fact: A large P value (not statistically significant) does not prove there is no effect, because a low-powered study can miss a real difference, so the evidence is insufficient to decide whether one treatment is better.

A P value of 0.4 does not show that either treatment works. The 10 percentage point difference (30 percent versus 20 percent) could easily have arisen by chance, so no effectiveness can be claimed for either arm from this result alone.
A nonsignificant result does not prove that neither treatment works. The trial may simply have been too small (low power) to detect a real difference, so absence of proof of an effect is not proof of no effect.
expls.The statistical power of this study is 6: Power cannot be read from a P value. Power is 1 minus the probability of a type II error and depends on sample size, effect size, event rate and the chosen alpha; the P value of 0.4 gives no information about it.
expls.The best estimate of treatment effect si: The value 0.4 is the P value, a probability, not an effect size. The observed effect is a 10 percentage point higher remission rate (30 percent minus 20 percent), or a ratio of 1.5, and the P value shows only that chance could explain it.
expls.There is insufficient information to dec: Correct. The P value of 0.4 is far above 0.05, so an effect is not established, but it also cannot exclude a real, clinically important effect that a study with too little power missed. The evidence is inconclusive in either direction.

11.3.correct: There is insufficient information to decide whether one treatment is better than the other.

11.4.guide_fact: A 95% confidence interval is a range of values, with boundaries called confidence limits, that should contain the true value with 95% confidence; it shows the statistical precision of an estimate.

expls.The association is not statistically sig: The interval 1.05 to 2.07 does not contain 1.0, the value that means no effect for a relative risk, so the result is statistically significant at the 0.05 level (although only just, since the lower limit is barely above 1).
expls.A strong association between vitamin A i: A relative risk of 1.48 is a modest association, and the lower limit of 1.05 is barely above no effect. Confidence intervals show precision, not proof; this is also a cohort study, so confounding and other bias could still explain it.
expls.The statistical power of this study is 9: The 95 percent in a confidence interval is the confidence level, not power. Power is the probability of detecting a real difference (1 minus the type II error probability) and cannot be read from an interval.
expls.There is a 95% chance that a range of re: Correct. A 95 percent confidence interval is a range of values (here relative risks from 1.05 to 2.07) that should contain the true value, with 95 percent confidence. It shows the precision of the estimate.
expls.Bias is an unlikely explanation for this: A confidence interval addresses only random error, meaning chance. Bias, such as recall or measurement bias, and confounding are separate problems that a narrow or significant interval does not remove.

11.4.correct: There is a 95% chance that a range of relative risks as low as 1.05 and as high as 2.07 includes the true risk.

11.5.guide_fact: P less than 0.05 is generally accepted as statistically significant, but this is an arbitrary number; it is a useful convention rather than a mathematical or clinical boundary.

expls.It definitively rules out a false-positi: A P value of 0.05 or less does not rule out a false positive. P = 0.05 means about 1 chance in 20 that a difference this big arose by chance, so a type I error (false positive) can still occur.
expls.It is an arbitrarily chosen but useful r: Correct. The 0.05 cutoff is an arbitrary number that researchers agreed on by convention. It is useful as a rule of thumb, but it has no special mathematical or clinical meaning.
The P value concerns type I error (false positive). Type II error is a false negative, a separate concept tied to statistical power, and a significance threshold does not rule it out.
expls.It is a way of establishing a clinically: Statistical significance says nothing about how large or clinically important an effect is. A tiny difference can have P < 0.05, especially in a large trial, and still be irrelevant to practice.
expls.Larger or smaller P values do not provid: Other P values are informative: smaller values (0.01, 0.001) mean chance is a less likely explanation, and larger values mean it is more likely. The 0.05 cutoff is just a convention for calling a result significant.

11.5.correct: It is an arbitrarily chosen but useful rule of thumb.

11.6.guide_fact: Multivariable modeling lets investigators examine the effect of one variable on the outcome while taking the effects of many other variables (confounders and effect modifiers) into account at the same time.

expls.Models can control for many variables si: Correct. Multivariable modeling examines the effect of two or more variables together, so it can take many other variables (confounders or effect modifiers) into account at the same time, which stratified analysis cannot do easily.
expls.Models do not depend on assumptions abou: Models depend heavily on assumptions about the data, such as normality and independent errors, and their validity rests on those assumptions holding. That is a limitation, not an advantage.
expls.There is a standardized and reproducible: There is no single standardized way to build a model. Investigators choose which variables to include and which assumptions to make, so two teams can build different models from the same data.
expls.Models make stratified analyses unnecess: Models complement stratified analyses rather than replacing them. Models are also poor at identifying effect modification, which stratifying by the variable makes visible, so stratified analyses remain necessary.
expls.Models can control for confounding in la: In a large randomized trial, randomization has already made confounding very unlikely, so modeling adds little. Modeling matters most in observational studies, where groups are not balanced by chance.

11.6.correct: Models can control for many variables simultaneously.

11.7.guide_fact: To have a good (about 95%) chance of observing at least one event, the number of people observed should be about 3 divided by the event rate, so a trial with 15,000 treated people can detect a side effect occurring in about 1 in 5,000.

expls.1/5,000: Correct. Only about 15,000 people (half of 30,000) receive chemoprevention. The rule of thumb is that observing at least one event needs about 3 divided by the event rate in people; 3 divided by 15,000 is 1 in 5,000, which gives about a 95 percent chance of seeing at least one case.
expls.1/10,000: This uses all 30,000 participants (3 divided by 30,000). Only the 15,000 in the chemoprevention arm are exposed to the drug, so at 1 in 10,000 the chance of seeing even one case is only about 78 percent.
expls.1/15,000: At 1 in 15,000 the expected number of events among 15,000 treated people is only 1, giving about a 63 percent chance of seeing at least one, well short of a good chance. It would need about 45,000 treated people.
expls.1/20,000: At 1 in 20,000 the expected number of events in 15,000 treated people is about 0.75, giving roughly a 53 percent chance of seeing at least one. That is little better than a coin flip.
expls.1/30,000: At 1 in 30,000 the expected number of events among 15,000 treated people is only 0.5, giving about a 39 percent chance of seeing at least one. Rarer side effects generally escape notice in trials of this size.

11.8.guide_fact: In a noninferiority trial the margin is the largest difference judged clinically unimportant, so when the true difference is significantly less than the margin, the new treatment is unlikely to be worse than the established one.
cites: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

expls.There was no clinically important differ: Correct. The margin of 8 points is the investigators' judgment of a clinically important difference. The observed difference of 3.6 is below it and the noninferiority test rejected the null hypothesis that physical therapy is worse, so no clinically important difference exists.
expls.There was a statistically significant gr: The reported P value tests noninferiority against the 8-point margin, not whether surgery is better than physical therapy. No test of superiority is reported, and a 3.6-point difference is smaller than the 8 points judged clinically important.
expls.The study could not reject the null hypo: The study did reject the null hypothesis. In this design the null hypothesis is that the alternative treatment is worse than the established one by the margin or more; a P value of 0.001, under the one-sided 0.025 level, rejected it.
expls.The study may have erroneously concluded: The study did not conclude that a true difference exists; it concluded that physical therapy is not worse than surgery by the 8-point margin. The only error that conclusion could carry is a false claim of noninferiority (type I error), limited by the preset one-sided alpha of 0.025.
expls.A smaller margin would have been more li: A smaller margin makes noninferiority harder to show. With a margin under 3.6, the observed difference would exceed the margin, so the null hypothesis that physical therapy is worse could not be rejected. Small margins also call for larger samples.

11.8.correct: There was no clinically important difference between surgery and physical therapy.

11.9.guide_fact: Statistical power (1 minus the probability of a type II error) depends jointly on effect size, the event rate in the control group and the type I and type II error levels; the choice of statistical test matters least.

expls.Effect size: Effect size is directly tied to power. A larger true difference between groups is easier to detect, so power rises with effect size and a small expected effect needs more patients.
expls.Type I error: Type I error (alpha) is directly tied to power. Setting a stricter threshold, such as 0.01 instead of 0.05, makes a significant result harder to reach and lowers power unless the sample size is increased.
expls.Rate of outcome events in the control gr: The control-group event rate is directly tied to power. With a dichotomous outcome, more events give more information, so a low rate of events in the control group lowers power.
expls.Type II error: Type II error is directly tied to power, because power equals 1 minus the probability of a type II error. A type II error probability of 0.20 gives a power of 0.80.
expls.The statistical test used: Correct. The statistical test used can change the calculated power slightly but is not a main determinant. Power depends mainly on effect size, event rate, the type I error level and the type II error level, which together set sample size.

11.10.guide_fact: A multivariable prediction model keeps the variables that each improve prediction of the outcome, so those variables are the risk factors for it; such a model still needs independent validation.

expls.The positive predictive values can be ca: Positive predictive value depends on prevalence as well as sensitivity and specificity. Prevalence of postoperative death is not given, so positive predictive values cannot be calculated from those characteristics alone.
expls.The model performance indicates that it: Good performance in the derivation cohort does not show the model is useful for risk stratification. It has only been checked internally, so it needs independent validation in other populations before use.
expls.Asthma is a confounder and thus excluded: Asthma is not a confounder here. A confounder is linked to both an exposure and the outcome and is adjusted for. In a prediction model, asthma was simply left out because it did not improve the prediction.
expls.Age confounds the other model variables: Age is a variable that improves the prediction of mortality, so it belongs in the model. Removing it would weaken prediction. Confounding describes a distorted exposure-outcome relationship, not variables that jointly predict.
expls.Age, creatinine, and ejection fraction a: Correct. A prediction model keeps the variables that each improve prediction of the outcome, so age, creatinine and ejection fraction are risk factors for postoperative mortality in this study, and asthma is not.

11.10.correct: Age, creatinine, and ejection fraction are risk factors for postoperative mortality in this study.

11.11.guide_fact: Bayesian reasoning is about how new information (each new study's results) changes a prior belief, so belief in a treatment effect after a study differs from belief before it.
cites: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13

expls.Prior belief in the comparative effectiv: Equipoise is the ethical basis for randomizing: there is no conclusive evidence that either treatment is better, so randomization is acceptable. It is not what Bayesian reasoning is about, which is how new evidence revises belief.
expls.The results of each new study change bel: Correct. Bayesian reasoning starts from a prior belief about the treatment effect and updates it with each new study, so belief after the study differs from belief before it. The same idea appears when a test result changes pretest probability into post-test probability.
expls.Bayesian inference is an alternative way: Bayesian inference is not another way of calculating a P value. A P value is the probability of a result as large as observed by chance if there is no difference; Bayesian reasoning instead updates prior belief with new data.
expls.Bayesian reasoning is based, like infere: Basing conclusions on the null hypothesis of no difference is the approach of frequentist inferential statistics, which uses P values. Bayesian reasoning updates prior beliefs, so it is not built on the null hypothesis.
expls.Bayesian reasoning depends on a well-def: A well-defined hypothesis before the study describes standard hypothesis testing. Bayesian reasoning is defined by revising a prior belief with new evidence, which is not the same as requiring a hypothesis stated in advance.

11.11.correct: The results of each new study change belief in treatment effect from what it was before the study.

11.12.guide_fact: A confidence interval gives the point estimate and the range of values likely to include the true effect, so it carries more information than a P value alone; an interval excluding no effect (hazard ratio of 1.0) matches P less than 0.05.

expls.The results are consistent with almost n: This statement is true, so it is not the answer. The lower limit of 1.01 is barely above 1.0 (no effect), so the data are compatible with an increase in death rate of only about 1 percent.
expls.The best estimate of treatment effect is: This statement is true, so it is not the answer. The best estimate of the effect is the point estimate, a hazard ratio of 1.22, which lies inside the interval and means about a 22 percent higher death rate with intensive treatment.
expls.If a P value were calculated, the result: This statement is true, so it is not the answer. The interval 1.01 to 1.46 excludes 1.0, the value meaning no effect, so a P value would be below 0.05.
expls.A P value would provide as much informat: Correct. This statement is not true. A P value tells only whether chance is a plausible explanation. The interval also gives the point estimate and the range of effects consistent with the data, so it carries more information.
expls.The results are consistent with 46% high: This statement is true, so it is not the answer. The upper confidence limit of 1.46 means the results are consistent with a death rate up to 46 percent higher in the intensively treated group.

11.12.correct: A P value would provide as much information as the confidence interval.

12.1.guide_fact: Experimental studies of risk in humans are limited by ethical constraints, so a randomized trial of a possibly harmful exposure such as cell phone use is unlikely and observational designs are used instead.
cites: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13
8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

A randomized trial of this question would be expensive, and cost is a listed limitation of trials, but it is not the main obstacle; a large study can be funded, whereas assigning people to a possibly harmful exposure cannot be done at any price.
expls.People would not agree to be randomized: Correct. Randomly assigning people to a potentially harmful exposure such as heavy cell phone use is an ethical problem, and people would not accept long-term restrictions on using their phones. Experimental studies of risk in humans are limited by ethical constraints, so observational designs are used instead.
Time is a practical limitation of trials, and a cancer with a long latency would need long follow-up, but that is a difficulty and not the main barrier; the decisive barrier is that people cannot ethically or realistically be randomized to a possibly harmful exposure.
expls.Even if done well, a randomized trial co: This is false. A well-done randomized trial is the strongest design for showing cause and effect because random assignment balances other factors between groups; the reason no such trial is likely here is ethics and willingness to participate, not an inability of the design to answer the question.

12.1.correct: People would not agree to be randomized to cell phone use.

12.2.guide_fact: Specificity (one cause leading to one effect) carries less weight than the other criteria listed, so an exposure associated with many different cancers is only weakly inconsistent with cause; many established causes, such as cigarette smoking, produce several diseases.

expls.A dose–response relationship: A dose-response relationship (larger exposure, higher rate of disease) would be consistent with cell phones causing brain cancer, because it is one of the criteria that raise belief in causation.
expls.A large effect size (such as relative ri: A large effect size, such as a large relative risk, would be consistent with cause, because strength of the association is one of the criteria for causality and large associations are harder to explain by confounding alone.
expls.Separate analyses of patients with right: Analyzing tumors by the side of the head where the phone is usually held would test the hypothesis directly; tumors clustering on the exposed side would support causation, and this kind of check bears on the causal criteria, making a cause more or less believable.
expls.A biologic explanation for why cell phon: A biologic explanation for how phones might cause cancer would support the hypothesis, because biologic plausibility is one of the criteria for causality (the relationship makes sense biologically).
expls.Cell phone use is associated with many d: Correct. An exposure associated with many different cancers lacks specificity (one cause leading to one effect), which counts for less than the other criteria listed; many well-established causes, such as cigarette smoking, produce several diseases, so lack of specificity only weakly argues against a cause.

12.2.correct: Cell phone use is associated with many different kinds of cancers

12.3.guide_fact: Most diseases, such as coronary heart disease, have multiple interacting causes (a web of causation); a risk factor is neither sufficient nor necessary by itself.

expls.Tuberculosis has a single cause, the tub: Not correct. The tubercle bacillus is a necessary cause (without it, tuberculosis cannot occur), but it is not sufficient: many exposed people never develop the disease, so host and environmental factors also matter. A necessary cause that is present may or may not lead to disease.
expls.Most genetic diseases are caused only by: Not correct. Nearly all diseases are caused by the joint effect of genes and environment, so an abnormal gene is usually only one contributor; even in single-gene disorders, whether and how severely disease appears often depends on other genes and environmental exposures, which is the web-of-causation view.
expls.Coronary heart disease has multiple inte: Correct. Coronary heart disease is caused by several risk factors acting together, a web of causation with multiple causes. A risk factor raises the probability of disease in a group and is neither necessary nor sufficient by itself.
expls.Effective treatment has been the main ca: Not correct. Tuberculosis rates fell steeply long before effective drug treatment became available in the 1950s, so treatment cannot be the main cause of the decline; other factors, such as living conditions, were changing the rate.

12.3.correct: Coronary heart disease has multiple interacting causes.

12.4.guide_fact: The criteria for causality are temporality, strength, dose-response, reversibility, consistency, biologic plausibility, specificity and analogy; statistical significance is not among them because it addresses only chance.

expls.Dose–response: Dose-response is one of the criteria for causality: a larger exposure leading to a higher rate of disease supports a cause-and-effect relationship, so it does belong on the list.
expls.Statistical significance: Correct. Statistical significance is not a causal criterion. It only shows that an association is unlikely to be due to chance, whereas the causal criteria (temporality, strength, dose-response, reversibility, consistency, biologic plausibility, specificity, analogy) judge whether an association is cause and effect.
expls.Reversibility: Reversibility is one of the criteria for causality: decreased exposure leading to less disease supports a cause-and-effect relationship, so it does belong on the list.
expls.Biologic plausibility: Biologic plausibility is one of the criteria for causality: the relationship should make sense biologically, so it does belong on the list.
expls.Analogy: Analogy is one of the criteria for causality: a similar cause and effect pattern for a similar exposure and disease supports cause, so it does belong on the list.

12.5.guide_fact: Cost-effectiveness analysis describes financial costs per clinical effect, such as cost per year of life saved, for alternative tests and treatments.

expls.Cost–benefit analysis: Cost-benefit analysis expresses both the costs and the benefits in money. This study reports its result per year of life saved, a clinical effect and not a dollar value, so it is not cost-benefit analysis.
expls.Decision analysis: Decision analysis is a method of comparing the possible outcomes of alternative choices; it is not the name for a study reporting a cost per unit of clinical benefit, which is what $20,000 per year of life saved describes.
expls.Cost-effectiveness analysis: Correct. Cost-effectiveness analysis describes financial costs per clinical effect, here dollars per year of life saved, for alternative tests or treatments (here fecal occult blood testing compared with no screening).
expls.A clinical decision rule: A clinical decision rule is a tool that helps clinicians reach a decision from patient findings; it does not measure the cost of an intervention per year of life saved, so it does not describe this study.

12.6.guide_fact: Ecologic (aggregate) studies are subject to the ecologic fallacy: applying aggregate group data to an individual, when the affected individuals in an exposed group may not be the ones who were actually exposed.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

expls.Aggregate risk studies are not susceptib: This is false. Studies that compare groups are still vulnerable to confounding, because other characteristics of the groups can differ along with the exposure, and averaging across a group hides which individuals carry those other factors.
expls.Multiple time-series studies cannot prov: This is too absolute. Time-series studies, which follow a rate before and after a change, can support cause when other explanations, such as other changes in local conditions at the same time, have been ruled out; they are not automatically weak.
expls.Studies relating average exposure to ave: This is false. When exposure and disease are measured as group averages, the people who got the disease may not be the ones who were exposed, so such studies are better for generating hypotheses than for a strong test of cause.
expls.An ecological fallacy might affect their: Correct. Aggregate (ecologic) studies measure exposure and disease in groups, not individuals, so the ecologic fallacy is possible: applying group-level data to an individual, when the affected people may not have been the exposed ones.

12.6.correct: An ecological fallacy might affect their validity.

12.7.guide_fact: In a time-series study, a change in disease rate after an intervention may be caused by other changes at about the same time, so alternative explanations must be ruled out before concluding the intervention caused it.

expls.Better antibiotics became available arou: Correct. Better antibiotics arriving at about the same time is another change that could explain the decline, and the alternative explanations for an association must be excluded before the program can be credited. In a time-series study, changes in local conditions at about the same time weaken the causal conclusion.
expls.Hand washing, a part of the MRSA package: More hand washing after the program began would strengthen the belief in cause, because it shows the program's components were carried out and fits a biologically plausible route by which the package lowers infections.
expls.The rate of MRSA infections was stable f: A stable rate before the program would strengthen the belief in cause, because the decline is then a new change and not the continuation of a downward trend that was already under way (in the graph the rate fluctuated without falling before the program).
expls.Decline in rates began just after the pr: A decline that began just after the program started fits the temporal relationship, the cause preceding the effect, which is a criterion for causality, so it would strengthen and not weaken belief in cause.

12.7.correct: Better antibiotics became available around the time of the program.

12.8.guide_fact: Randomized controlled trials are the strongest evidence for cause and effect, but many suspected causes cannot be studied with one because experimental studies of harm are limited by ethics and willingness to participate.
cites: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13

expls.Clinical trials may not be ethical or fe: Correct. Randomized trials are the strongest design for cause and effect when done well, but they are often impossible because studies of harm are unethical and people may be unwilling to take part. Experimental studies of risk in humans are limited by ethical constraints.
expls.Randomized trials cannot control for unm: This is not accurate. Random assignment is what lets a trial balance unmeasured as well as measured factors between groups, which is why it is the strongest design; only small trials may show residual confounding by chance, and that is not the main limitation.
expls.Type of study design is only a crude mea: Design type is indeed only a rough guide to strength, but that caveat applies to the ranking of all designs and is not a limitation specific to trials. The question asks about the main limitation of trials for establishing cause, which is that they are frequently unethical or infeasible.
expls.Results of poorly designed and conducted: Poorly designed or conducted trials can indeed be weak, but that reflects execution and not the design. A well-designed and well-conducted trial remains the strongest evidence; the main limitation is that trials cannot be done for many suspected causes.

12.8.correct: Clinical trials may not be ethical or feasible for some questions.

12.9.guide_fact: The more criteria for causality that are met, the stronger the evidence for cause and effect; the pattern across all criteria is more powerful than any single one.

expls.Observational studies that have controll: Observational studies that control bias and chance are needed, but they show an association; they still leave open whether it is cause and effect, which requires considering the causal criteria together.
expls.A biologic mechanism can explain the rel: A biologic mechanism, biologic plausibility, is one criterion for causality and supports a cause, but by itself it is weaker than the whole pattern of evidence.
expls.The purported cause clearly precedes the: Temporality, the cause preceding the effect, is necessary for causation, but it is only one criterion; a cause coming first does not by itself show the exposure produced the outcome.
A dose-response relationship raises belief in cause, but it is a single criterion; it is stronger when combined with the others than when it stands alone.
expls.The evidence as a whole is consistent wi: Correct. The more criteria for causality that are met, the stronger the case for cause and effect; the pattern of evidence across all the criteria is more powerful than evidence for any one of them.

12.9.correct: The evidence as a whole is consistent with the Bradford Hill criteria.

12.10.guide_fact: cites: ["9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14", "9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 11"]

expls.Use of cell phones increases the inciden: This result is consistent with a 50% increase, because the upper confidence limit of 1.5 corresponds to a 50% higher risk; the interval includes values that would mean harm.
expls.Use of cell phones protects against brai: This result is consistent with protection, because the lower confidence limit of 0.6 corresponds to a 40% lower risk; the interval includes values that would mean benefit.
expls.Specific types of cancers might be assoc: This result is consistent with specific types being associated, because the estimate pools all brain cancers together, and a risk in one subtype could be hidden by the combined analysis.
expls.The study has adequate statistical power: Correct (this is the statement that does not fit). An interval of 0.6 to 1.5 is wide, running from clear benefit to clear harm, which shows imprecision and too little statistical power; a study with adequate power would give a narrower interval, so the null result cannot be trusted as showing no association.

12.10.correct: The study has adequate statistical power to answer the research question.

13.1.guide_fact: The main advantage of combining (pooling) study results in a meta-analysis is a larger sample size, which gives a more precise estimate of effect size than any single study.
cites: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22

expls.You wish to obtain a more generalizable: Pooling can make the conclusion somewhat more generalizable because results come from more than one time and place, but that is not the main reason to combine studies. The main gain is statistical: a larger combined sample gives a more precise estimate.
expls.A statistical test shows that the studie: A statistical test showing heterogeneity is a reason for caution, not a rationale for pooling. Studies to be combined must be similar, and a significant heterogeneity test means the effect sizes differ more than chance allows, so pooling is questionable or needs a random effects approach.
expls.Most of the component studies are statis: Whether the component studies are individually statistically significant is not a reason to combine them. Pooling is done to improve precision and power, which matters most when single studies are too small to be conclusive on their own.
expls.The component studies have different, an: Pooling does not cancel biases. A meta-analysis is only as good as the studies it includes, and biases shared by observational studies, such as confounding, carry into the summary estimate, so complementary biases are not a justification for combining.
expls.You can obtain a more precise estimate o: Correct. Meta-analysis weights and pools the numerical results of similar studies, so the larger combined sample gives a stronger, more precise estimate of effect size (a narrower confidence interval) than any single study can.

13.1.correct: You can obtain a more precise estimate of effect size.

13.2.guide_fact: MEDLINE can be searched by both content and methods terms, which is a strength; its limitations are missed articles, incomplete coverage of the world's journals, and publication bias, so reviewers should also use complementary search methods.

expls.Studies with negative results tend to no: This is a real limitation. Research without statistically significant results is less likely to be published, so a search of published literature misses those studies and tilts the evidence toward positive findings; a database search cannot correct it.
expls.MEDLINE searches typically miss some art: This is a real limitation. Even for articles that are in MEDLINE, a search will not retrieve every relevant one, so a reviewer relying on a single search strategy can overlook eligible studies.
expls.MEDLINE does not include all of the worl: This is a real limitation. MEDLINE covers a large share of the medical literature but not all of the world's journals, so relevant studies published elsewhere are missed unless other databases and sources are also searched.
expls.MEDLINE can be simultaneously searched f: Correct, this is the exception. Being able to search MEDLINE for both the content area and study methods at once is a strength that helps narrow a search, not a limitation. The limitations are missed articles, incomplete journal coverage, and publication bias.

13.2.correct: MEDLINE can be simultaneously searched for both content area and methods.

13.3.guide_fact: Pooling data on individual patients rather than whole trials makes subgroup analyses possible, because combined patient-level data give enough people in each subgroup and avoid the ecologic fallacy of group-level comparisons.

Ecological comparisons compare group-level characteristics, which risks applying aggregate data to individuals (the ecologic fallacy). Pooling individual patients does the opposite and lets analysis be done at the level of the person, which avoids that problem.
expls.It is more efficient for the investigato: Efficiency is not the benefit of pooling patients instead of trials. The gain is analytic, in that combined patient-level data can be analyzed in ways summary results cannot, most notably by subgroup.
Correct. Individual trials are usually too small to examine subgroups, but pooling patients from several trials gives enough people in each subgroup to compare effects, and meta-analysis is noted for detecting differences in subgroups. This works only when patients, not trials, are pooled.
expls.It is not necessary to choose between fi: The choice between the fixed effect model and the random effects model depends on whether the studies show heterogeneity (fixed effect when there is none, random effects when it is present), and pooling patients does not remove the need to consider it.
Publication bias arises because studies without significant results are less likely to be published. Pooling individual patients from the trials that are available does not bring in unpublished trials, so this approach does not by itself make publication bias less likely.

13.4.guide_fact: A specific clinical question is defined by PICO (patients, intervention, comparison, outcomes); covariates are not part of the question.

expls.Covariates that were taken into account: Correct. A specific clinical question is defined by PICO: patients, intervention, comparison, and outcomes. Covariates are not part of the question; they bear on how well the question can be answered, such as by confounding or effect modification.
expls.Interventions (e.g., exposure or experim: The intervention or exposure is the I in PICO (patients, intervention, comparison, outcomes): the main intervention, prognostic factor, or exposure being considered. It is used to define the clinical question.

13.5.guide_fact: A systematic review should describe each study's characteristics and risk of bias so readers can judge the strength of the conclusions, whereas combining quality items into a single summary score is less well established.

expls.The validity of summary measures of stud: Combining individual quality items into one summary score is less well established than describing them, in part because it is not meaningful to give every element the same weight. Scoring systems exist but their validity is not settled.
expls.A description of study quality is a usef: Correct. A good systematic review describes each included study's characteristics and risk of bias, so readers can judge how strong the conclusions are. Assessing the quality of the included studies is a standard step in evaluating a review.
expls.In a summary measure of quality, strengt: A summary score adds strengths and weaknesses together, but a strength in one area does not repair a fatal weakness in another. A flaw such as failure to randomize can still distort the result no matter how large the sample is.
expls.Individual measures of quality such as r: Quality elements such as randomization and blinding are assessed precisely because weaknesses can bias results. For example, blinding of participants protects against performance bias, so these features are tied to how trustworthy the results are.

13.5.correct: A description of study quality is a useful part of systematic reviews.

13.6.guide_fact: Small studies that find no effect are the least likely to be published, which produces publication bias; large studies tend to be published whatever they find.

expls.Small positive studies: Small studies with positive results are more likely to be published than small studies with no effect, because research with statistically significant results is favored for publication. They are not the least likely to be published.
expls.Large negative studies: Large studies tend to be published whatever they find, because of their size and importance, so a large negative study is not among the least likely to be published.
expls.Large positive studies: Large positive studies are very likely to be published, since both size and a significant result favor publication.
expls.Small negative studies: Correct. Research without statistically significant results is less likely to be published, and small studies do not carry enough weight to overcome this, whereas large studies are usually published regardless of their findings. This is the core of publication bias.

13.7.guide_fact: Narrative reviews can cover broad topics and a range of issues, but they are unstructured and may not transparently describe how the evidence was selected or critique it.

expls.Readers can confirm that evidence cited: This describes a systematic review, not a narrative review. Systematic reviews use explicit inclusion criteria and list excluded studies so readers can check selection. In narrative reviews cited articles may have been selected to prove a point of view.
expls.Narrative reviews can review a broad ran: Correct. Narrative reviews can address broad topics and a range of issues, such as the whole set of questions involved in caring for a condition. The cost is an unstructured approach with no transparent description of how the evidence was chosen.
expls.They rely on the experience and judgment: Authors' clinical experience is a real feature of narrative reviews, but it cuts both ways, because information may then be shaped by the authors' values and personal experience. The advantage that systematic reviews cannot match is covering a broad range of questions bearing on the care of a condition.
expls.They provide a quantitative summary of e: A quantitative summary of effects is a feature of meta-analysis, which weights and pools numerical results from similar studies. Narrative reviews are unstructured and typically do not calculate a summary effect.
expls.The scientific strength of the studies c: Explicit evaluation of the scientific strength of studies is a feature of systematic reviews, which describe each study's risk of bias. Narrative reviews may not include a critique of the original research.

13.7.correct: Narrative reviews can review a broad range of questions bearing on the care of a condition.
13.7.conflict: The lecture lists author experience as an advantage of narrative reviews, so the option about relying on expert judgment is also arguably an advantage of narrative reviews; the keyed answer (broad range of questions) is kept because it is the advantage systematic reviews cannot match.

13.8.guide_fact: A forest plot always shows each study's point estimate, confidence interval, and weight, but a pooled summary effect (the diamond) is shown only if pooling is justified.

expls.The number of studies that meet inclusio: The studies included in the review each appear on the plot, one row per study, so the number of included studies is visible; this is part of how a forest plot summarizes the raw evidence. It is not the element that is sometimes left out.
expls.A summary or pooled effect size with con: Correct. A pooled (summary) effect with its confidence interval, shown as a diamond, is included only if pooling is justified. If the studies are too different, the plot shows the individual studies without combining them.
expls.Point estimates of effect size for each: The point estimate of effect size for each study is always shown, typically as a square or dot, and is a basic element of a forest plot.
expls.Confidence intervals for each study: Each study's confidence interval is always shown as a horizontal line through its point estimate, so it is a standard element of every forest plot.
expls.The size or weight contributed by each s: The size or weight each study contributes is always conveyed, usually by the size of the marker, because studies are weighted in proportion to their size.

13.8.correct: A summary or pooled effect size with confidence interval

13.9.guide_fact: Severity of illness cannot be controlled for in a study-level meta-analysis; it can be explored by subgroup analysis, sensitivity analysis, or metaregression across studies, or by patient-level analyses.

expls.Controlling for severity of illness in a: Correct. In a study-level meta-analysis only summary data from each study are available, so you cannot control for a covariate such as severity of illness as could be done in a single study or in a patient-level analysis. You can only compare studies with different average severities.
expls.A mathematical model relating average se: Relating average severity of illness to the outcome across the studies is metaregression, a recognized way to explore reasons for differences between studies (heterogeneity) at the study level.
expls.A comparison of summary effect sizes in: Comparing summary effects in studies grouped by mean severity is a subgroup analysis, which is one of the recognized ways to identify the reasons for differences between studies.
expls.Subgroup analyses of patient-level data: Subgroup analyses of patient-level data are possible because the individual patients can be separated by severity, which is one advantage of pooling patients rather than trials.

13.9.correct: Controlling for severity of illness in a study-level meta-analysis

13.10.guide_fact: Studies can be combined into a single summary effect when the patients, interventions, and outcomes are relatively similar, because a meta-analysis may be misleading if the included studies are not similar.

expls.A statistical test does not detect heter: A nonsignificant heterogeneity test is not reassurance with only five studies, because the test has low power to detect differences among so few studies. Pooling is justified by whether the studies are actually similar.
Studies can all be of high quality yet differ in the patients enrolled, the interventions given, or the outcomes measured. Quality does not make dissimilar studies combinable.
expls.The patients, interventions, and outcome: Correct. Studies must be similar in order to be pooled, and this is judged by informed review of the patients, interventions, and outcomes rather than by a statistic alone. Combining dissimilar studies can be misleading.
expls.Publication bias has been ruled out by a: A funnel plot assesses publication and reporting bias, not clinical similarity. Even a reassuring funnel plot would not show that the patients, interventions, and outcomes are similar enough to combine.
expls.The random effects model will be used to: A random effects model is a way to calculate the summary once pooling is decided, and it allows for variation among studies. It does not make dissimilar studies suitable for combining, because pooling studies that are not similar can still mislead.

13.10.correct: The patients, interventions, and outcomes are relatively similar.

13.11.guide_fact: Network meta-analyses can use observational or randomized data and study-level or patient-level data, and the interventions can be diverse as long as they address similar patients and outcomes.

expls.Multiple interventions are directly comp: Network meta-analyses can rank several interventions, but the comparisons are not all direct. Many are inferred indirectly through a shared comparator, so the network combines direct and indirect evidence rather than comparing every intervention head to head.
expls.They require individual-level patient da: They do not require individual-level data. Network meta-analyses can use study-level or patient-level data, so this requirement is false.
expls.They require randomized controlled trial: They do not require randomized controlled trials. Network meta-analyses can use observational or randomized data, so this requirement is false.
expls.They do not require similar intervention: Correct. The interventions in a network meta-analysis can be diverse. What matters is that the studies address similar patients and similar outcomes, which allows both direct and indirect comparisons among the interventions or tests.
expls.They show the additional effects of new: Showing the added effect of each new study on the summary estimate describes a cumulative meta-analysis, which adds studies one at a time. A network meta-analysis compares multiple interventions.

13.11.correct: They do not require similar interventions for analysis.

13.12.guide_fact: The random effects model allows for variation among studies that is not due to chance, so it is used when heterogeneity is present and gives wider, more realistic confidence intervals than the fixed effect model.
cites: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23

expls.It can be used for studies with time-to-: Both models can be applied to time-to-event outcomes, so this is not a special advantage of the random effects model. The choice between the two depends on the heterogeneity among studies, not on the type of outcome.
expls.It describes the summary effect size for: This describes the fixed effect model, which assumes a fixed magnitude of effect for one narrowly defined question, with variation attributed to chance. The random effects model allows for variation not due to chance.
expls.It is better suited for meta-analyses of: Suitability for diagnostic test performance is not what distinguishes the two models; the deciding factor is whether heterogeneity is present. The random effects model is used when it is, whatever the kind of study.
expls.Confidence intervals tend to be narrower: Random effects models give wider, not narrower, confidence intervals, because they account for variation between studies. The narrower intervals belong to the fixed effect model, which is why they can be falsely reassuring when studies differ.
expls.It gives more realistic results when the: Correct. The random effects model allows for variation among studies that is not due to chance, and so is used when heterogeneity is present. It gives wider confidence intervals that are more likely to be accurate than the narrower ones a fixed effect model would give.

13.12.correct: It gives more realistic results when there is heterogeneity among studies.

14.1.guide_fact: It is virtually impossible to keep up with all strong, clinically relevant new research on your own, so a publication or service that reviews the literature in your field is the most useful tool for keeping current.
cites: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 37

Journals are one way to keep current, but more than 30,000 medical journals and over 2 million studies exist, so a few subscriptions cannot cover all the strong, relevant new research; a service that screens and summarizes the literature does that work for you.
expls.Subscribe to a service that reviews the: Correct. It is virtually impossible to keep up with all scientifically strong, clinically relevant new research alone, so a service that reviews the literature in your field does the screening and summarizing for you, which matters most when few colleagues are nearby.
Printed textbooks are fixed at the time of printing, so they are prone to outdated evidence, a recognized challenge of evidence-based practice; a new edition does not track developments as they appear.
MEDLINE holds more than 19 million citations, so searching it at intervals is inefficient for surveillance; it suits looking up a specific question or a rare event, not routinely keeping up with a whole field.
expls.Keep up contacts with colleagues in your: Colleagues are a legitimate way to keep current, but the stem says few are nearby, and occasional calls or e-mail do not systematically capture new strong research the way a dedicated literature-review service does.

14.1.correct: Subscribe to a service that reviews the literature in your field.

14.2.guide_fact: General medical journals expose readers to the many dimensions of the profession, but they do not reliably answer immediate clinical questions, guarantee that you are current, or guarantee flawless information.

Journals mostly report single original studies and are not efficient for answering an immediate question; answers come better from systematic reviews, practice guidelines, or an evidence-based synopsis from a credible resource.
expls.Assure that you have kept up with the me: With more than 30,000 medical journals and over 2 million studies published, reading even the best general journals leaves large gaps, so they cannot assure you have kept up with the literature.
expls.Guarantee that the information they cont: Journals cannot guarantee that; a Lancet study linking the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine to autism was retracted after undisclosed financial conflicts and unapproved procedures came to light, and peer review helps but does not make articles flawless.
expls.Expose you to the many dimensions of you: Correct. The best general journals are a rich source of information on the many dimensions of being a physician, including history, politics, science, ideas, and experiences, even though they are not good for immediate answers or surveillance.

14.2.correct: Expose you to the many dimensions of your profession.

14.3.guide_fact: Good systematic reviews provide the highest level of evidence, while a single recent article taken out of context with other studies on the same question is of marginal value.

expls.A clinical practice guideline by a major: A good guideline gives its recommendations together with the supporting evidence and rationale, and trustworthy guidelines rest on systematic reviews, so a major society guideline is a credible source, not the least credible.
expls.A systematic review published in a major: Good systematic reviews and meta-analyses provide the highest level of evidence because they combine many studies to answer a specific, focused question, so a systematic review is among the most credible sources.
expls.The Cochrane Database of Systematic Revi: The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews belongs to the Cochrane Library, a listed evidence-based medicine resource named for Archie Cochrane, who advocated systematic reviews to verify treatment effectiveness, so it is a highly credible source, not the weakest.
expls.The most recent research article on this: Correct. A single recent article, seen out of context with the other studies on the same question, sits lower in the hierarchy than syntheses and is of marginal value unless it is much stronger than all the studies before it.

14.4.guide_fact: Searching MEDLINE and PubMed is indispensable for finding whether a rare event has been reported, but it is too inefficient for most questions at the point of care.

expls.Finding all of the best articles bearing: A MEDLINE search returns citations without grading their quality, and it is only one part of an effort to find every published article on a question, so a search alone does not find all of the best articles.
expls.An efficient strategy for finding the go: Searching a database of more than 19 million citations is inefficient for most questions at the point of care; a systematic review or an evidence-based synopsis from a credible resource is the faster route to good articles.
expls.Looking for reports of rare events: Correct. A targeted search is indispensable for learning whether a rare event has been reported, because a specific query can locate even a single case report among millions of citations; it is too inefficient for most questions at the point of care.
expls.Keeping up with the medical literature: The volume of literature (over 19 million MEDLINE citations) is far too large to keep up with by searching; keeping current is better done through a review service, professional organizations, and similar sources.
expls.Being familiar with the medical professi: Becoming familiar with the profession as a whole comes from reading broadly, such as general medical journals that cover its history, ideas, and experiences; a database search returns narrow citations on a topic.

14.4.correct: Looking for reports of rare events

14.5.guide_fact: Peer review helps limit bias and makes articles more accurate, readable, and complete, but published articles remain imperfect and readers must still judge their validity.

expls.Exclude articles by authors with a confl: Peer review does not exclude authors with conflicts of interest; conflicts are supposed to be disclosed so readers can judge whether bias is present, and the peer review process only helps limit their effects.
expls.Make the published article accurate and: Correct, as the best available answer. Peer review and editing make articles more readable, accurate, and complete, and it is an accepted marker of quality, but articles remain imperfect after publication.
expls.Relieve readers of the need to be skepti: Peer review does not relieve readers of skepticism; the retracted Lancet study on the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine was published, and readers must still judge the validity of the research and the strength of its methods.
expls.Decide for the editors about whether the: Peer reviewers only recommend that a manuscript be rejected, revised, or accepted; the editors review those recommendations and make the publication decision.

14.5.correct: Make the published article accurate and trustworthy.
14.5.conflict: The keyed wording 'accurate and trustworthy' overstates what peer review achieves; it is the best of the four options because it is the only one that describes a real benefit (better, more accurate articles), but peer review does not guarantee accuracy, and the explanations say so.

14.6.guide_fact: Conflict of interest can be financial, personal or intellectual, or institutional, and it exists in relation to a specific activity; investing in medical products in general, not tied to the topic studied, is not a conflict.

expls.Clinical income from performing colonosc: Income from performing colonoscopies is a financial conflict of interest, because the author benefits financially if colonoscopy is judged the best screening test.
expls.Investment in a company that makes colon: Owning stock in a company that makes colonoscopies is a financial conflict of interest, because the author would gain financially from a favorable conclusion about colonoscopy.
expls.Investment in medical products in genera: Correct. Conflict of interest relates to a specific activity, and investing in medical products in general is not tied to colonoscopy in particular, so it creates no specific conflict for this conclusion.
expls.Publications of articles that have consi: A record of publications consistently advocating colonoscopy is a personal, intellectual, and career conflict, because the author has a professional stake in the same conclusion being shown again.
expls.Rivalry with other scholars who advocate: Rivalry with scholars who favor another screening test is a personal and intellectual conflict, because a wish to defeat competing views can bias how the study is designed and reported.

14.6.correct: Investment in medical products in general

14.7.guide_fact: Subscribing to and keeping journals at hand is the least useful way to look up answers at the point of care, whereas guidelines, the Cochrane Library, and continually updated electronic references are valuable.

expls.Subscribing to several journals and keep: Correct. Journals have great value for other reasons, but a stack of them at the bedside is not a fast way to look up an answer, because they mostly report single studies rather than an organized, evidence-graded answer.
expls.Guidelines on http://www.guidelines.gov: Practice guidelines, including the government-sponsored collections that are listed among quality sources, give recommendations with supporting evidence and are a valuable point-of-care source, not the least useful.
expls.The Cochrane Library on the Internet: The Cochrane Library is a listed evidence-based medicine database of systematic reviews, so it is a valuable way to look up answers at the point of care, if a computer is available.
expls.A continually updated electronic textboo: A continually updated electronic textbook, of which UpToDate is a listed example, keeps recommendations current and is quick to search, so it is a valuable point-of-care source.

14.8.guide_fact: Judge a website by its sponsor, whether it gives facts and names its sources, and whether it is current, because an author's reputation alone does not show that the information is unbiased.

expls.The site is sponsored by a governmental: Government sponsorship together with a named advisory board is reassuring, because government databases are listed as quality sources and openly identified reviewers make the site transparent and accountable.
A site that provides facts instead of opinions is reassuring, because bias and the level of detail in the content are core parts of judging a source, and facts can be checked against a source.
expls.The primary source of information is sta: Stating the primary source of the information is reassuring, because a reader can verify the facts and judge their validity rather than trusting an unsupported claim.
expls.The date of the last revision is posted: A posted and recent revision date is reassuring, because a source must still be current, and outdated evidence is a recognized challenge in evidence-based practice.
expls.The author is a well-known expert in the: Correct. Fame alone is the least reassuring, because a well-known expert may still be biased; the retracted Lancet vaccine study came from an author with undisclosed conflicts. Look for the sponsoring organization, facts, and stated sources.

14.8.correct: The author is a well-known expert in the field.
14.8.conflict: The evaluating-websites method lists the author's credentials and expertise as one criterion, so an expert author is not worthless; the keyed answer is still the weakest of the five, because being well known is not the same as verified credentials, and it does not replace sponsor, facts, and stated sources.

14.9.guide_fact: Grading recommendations for treatment (GRADE, Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) rates the quality of evidence (A to C) and the strength of the recommendation (1 or 2) separately, weighing benefits against harms, and is most often applied to treatment and screening.

expls.Deciding whether to use a diagnostic tes: Correct. The grading table rates recommendations for treatment by the quality of the evidence and the strength of the recommendation; it is a way to grade evidence, and deciding whether to order a particular diagnostic test remains a clinical judgment rather than a component of the grading.
expls.Takes into account the balance of benefi: Weighing benefits against harms is part of grading; the clarity of risk and benefit determines whether a recommendation is strong or weak, and the process involves weighing pros and cons.
expls.Rates the quality of scientific evidence: Rating the quality of the evidence separately is part of grading; quality is the letter grade A to C, reflecting confidence in the estimate of effect, from high (well-performed randomized trials) to low (observational studies).
expls.Suggests how commonly and how forcefully: Suggesting how commonly and how forcefully to recommend a treatment is part of grading; a strong recommendation applies to most patients, whereas a weak one means the best action may differ by patient values.
expls.Rates the strength of the evidence and o: Rating the strength of the recommendation separately from the quality of the evidence is part of grading; strength is the number 1 or 2, so a strong recommendation can rest on low-quality evidence and a weak one on high-quality evidence.

14.9.correct: Deciding whether to use a diagnostic test

14.10.guide_fact: A comprehensive knowledge management plan combines browsing journals, a plan for looking up information at the point of care, a publication that keeps you current on new developments, and reliable web sites to recommend to patients.

expls.Subscribing to some journals and browsin: Subscribing to and browsing journals is one basic element of a comprehensive plan, but it is only part of it; the plan also needs point-of-care lookup, a review publication, and sites for patients.
expls.Establishing a plan for looking up infor: A plan for looking up information at the point of care is one basic element, but not the whole plan; keeping current and guiding patients to reliable sources are also needed.
expls.Finding a publication that helps you kee: A publication that helps you keep up with new developments is one basic element of a comprehensive plan, but not the whole plan; browsing, point-of-care lookup, and patient resources belong as well.
